title: Development of NanoBRET Cellular Target Engagement Assays in Primary Neurons for Activating Mutants of p21-Activated Kinase 1.
abstract: The p21-activated kinases (PAKs) are a group of serine-threonine kinases central to multiple signaling pathways that govern cell survival and proliferation. Aberrant activity of PAK1, the most well characterized member of the PAK family, drives progression of several malignancies and brain disorders, including Alzheimer's disease and neurodevelopmental disorders. Despite growing interest in PAK1 as a drug target for these diseases, there is no assay to evaluate the intracellular target engagement of PAK1 inhibitors. To address this need, we developed first-in-class NanoBRET assays for wild-type PAK1 and a neurodevelopmental disorder-causing gain-of-function PAK1 mutant. Furthermore, we executed our novel PAK1 NanoBRET assay to evaluate target engagement of PAK1 inhibitors in primary hippocampal neurons. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a NanoBRET cellular target engagement assay in primary neurons, thereby increasing the relevance of our work by confirming PAK1 inhibitor binding to the aberrant form of the protein in cerebral cells.

title: Cross-species molecular mapping of the photoreceptor sensory cilium and periciliary structures identifies conserved and species-specific architectural features.
abstract: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment. The microtubule-based ciliary axoneme extends from the basal body through the connecting cilium into the outer segment, thereby linking the inner and outer segments. Around this central axis, specialized periciliary structures are distributed across the apical inner segment and basal outer segment. Yet how these ciliary and periciliary structures differ between rods and cones and across mammals remains incompletely defined. Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we compared their nanoscale molecular organization across canine, non-human primate and human retinas. Key rod-cone differences in ciliary organization were broadly conserved among all three species, whereas the scale and morphology of individual ciliary subcompartments differed between species. Periciliary structures showed even greater species-specific diversification, particularly in rods. Human photoreceptors shared several structural features with non-human primate photoreceptors but also displayed inter-individual variability in accessory inner segment-like structure. These findings refine current understanding of photoreceptor sensory cilia and associated periciliary structures in large mammals, revealing that conserved rod-cone differences co-exist with pronounced species-specific structural and molecular specializations.

title: Cytoplasmic TDP-43 Accumulation in Autosomal Recessive Spastic Ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS) is a rare, early-onset neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity and peripheral neuropathy. It is caused by biallelic mutations in the SACS gene, which encodes sacsin, a large protein involved in cytoskeletal organization and mitochondrial homeostasis, and protein quality control. Despite advances in understanding sacsin biology, the molecular mechanisms underlying neurodegeneration in ARSACS remain incompletely understood. Here, we report the first neuropathological evidence of pathological TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) accumulation in ARSACS. METHODS: Available postmortem brain tissue from a genetically confirmed ARSACS patient homozygous for the Quebec founder mutation (SACS c.8844delT) was analyzed by immunohistochemistry, immunofluorescence and biochemical fractionation. RESULTS: Neurons in the prefrontal cortex, motor cortex and cerebellum exhibited cytoplasmic phosphorylated dot-like TDP-43 (pTDP-43) aggregates with reduced nuclear localization. Biochemical fractionation further identified detergent-insoluble TDP-43 species in ARSACS tissue. Additional pathological features included increased neurofilament accumulation, vacuole-like neuronal changes, Purkinje cell loss and p62-positive cytoplasmic inclusions. Similar dot-like cytoplasmic pTDP-43 aggregates were observed in a second ARSACS case. CONCLUSION: These findings identify pTDP-43 as a previously unrecognized pathological feature of ARSACS. While the patient exhibited no clinical or histopathological signs of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the presence of atypical pTDP-43 aggregates observed in ARSACS may represent a rare, secondary, early-stage or potentially underrecognized manifestation of TDP-43 pathology rather than a defining hallmark of the disease. Further studies in additional patients and experimental ARSACS models will be required to determine the prevalence and mechanistic basis of TDP-43 abnormalities in this disorder.
journal: The Canadian journal of neurological sciences. Le journal canadien des sciences neurologiques

title: Capsaicin suppresses microglial inflammation through TRPV1-SSR4 interaction.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) is increasingly recognized as an important regulator of microglial response during neuroinflammation, a key pathological feature of various neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease. Capsaicin, the primary pungent component in chili peppers, executes its anti-inflammatory properties as a TRPV1 agonist. Although the mechanism of TRPV1 channel activation and signal transduction by capsaicin has been extensively studied, the protein-protein interaction-based mechanisms by which TRPV1 modulates microglial inflammatory responses in the context of neurodegeneration remains unclear. METHODS: We used a lipopolysaccharide-induced acute neuroinflammation model to examine the effects of TRPV1 activation and pharmacological blockade of TRPV1 channel gating on microglial inflammatory responses. Proximity labeling-based proteomics, bioluminescence resonance energy transfer, and NanoLuc Binary Technology were used to identify and characterize TRPV1-interacting proteins. Signal sequence receptor subunit 4 (SSR4) knockdown and forced interaction between TRPV1 and SSR4 were performed to assess the functional contribution of the TRPV1-SSR4 interaction. Structural modeling, BRET-based domain mapping, and colocalization analyses were further used to examine the molecular and subcellular features of SSR4 recruitment by TRPV1. RESULTS: In the neuroinflammatory model, the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin attenuated pro-inflammatory cytokine production, neuronal apoptosis, microgliosis, and microglial soma enlargement in a TRPV1-dependent manner. Notably, pharmacological blockade of TRPV1 channel gating by capsazepine did not abolish the anti-inflammatory action of capsaicin, suggesting an alternative mechanism of action beyond the canonical ligand-gated Ca2⁺ influx. Screening of TRPV1 prey proteins and validation strategy identified SSR4 as a capsaicin-responsive, TRPV1-associated protein. SSR4 knockdown in microglia significantly diminished the suppression of inflammatory responses caused by TRPV1 activation. Conversely, forced interaction between TRPV1 and SSR4 partially mimicked the anti-inflammatory effects of TRPV1 activation. Further structural and cellular analyses suggested that the transmembrane region of TRPV1 supports SSR4 recruitment. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that capsaicin suppresses microglial inflammation mediated by the TRPV1-SSR4 interaction, providing new insights into the chemical biology basis of TRPV1 interoceptive signaling and potential applications of natural TRPV1 agonists for modifying therapy of neuroinflammation-associated neurodegeneration.

title: The landscape of gene loss and missense variation across the mammalian tree informs on gene essentiality.
abstract: Patterns of gene and sequence preservation across species provide insight into gene essentiality under natural selection. Here we developed two interspecies constraint metrics across 462 mammalian species: Gene Identity Score of Mammalian Orthologs (GISMO), which quantifies gene loss weighted by evolutionary distance to humans, and GISMO-mis, which measures missense constraint using the ratio of missense to synonymous variation across mammals. Both metrics are strongly correlated with human loss of function, missense and dosage constraint derived from large-scale sequencing studies, yet are largely independent of coding sequence length. GISMO and GISMO-mis identify essential genes missed by existing human-only metrics, particularly short genes. Genes in the most constrained deciles are enriched for rare variant associations in disorders linked to reduced fecundity, including schizophrenia, autism and neurodevelopmental disorders, and show strong enrichment for common variant heritability. These deciles also exhibit reduced copy number variation, consistent with dosage sensitivity. In addition, GISMO improves prioritization of recessive disease genes and captures signatures of homozygous selection across the mammalian tree. Taken together, GISMO and GISMO-mis leverage deep mammalian evolution to provide complementary, length-robust measures of gene essentiality that strengthen disease-gene prioritization and illuminate the selective forces shaping human biology.

title: Along-tract statistical mapping of white matter abnormalities in children with SeLECTS.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Emerging evidence suggests that self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS) may reflect atypical neurodevelopment. As WM maturation extends from the second trimester through adolescence, this study aimed to identify regions of delayed or aberrant white matter (WM) development in children with SeLECTS using along-tract statistical mapping for precise localization of microstructural alterations. MATERIALS AND METHODS: 38 children with SeLECTS and 31 healthy controls underwent diffusion-weighted MRI scan. Fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), and radial diffusivity (RD) were derived from the diffusion tensor model. Whole-brain tractography was performed using deterministic EuDX tracking and registered to a standardized bundle atlas in MNI space. Thirty WM tracts per subject were extracted. Linear mixed models within the BUAN tractometry framework were used to assess segment wise group differences, while partial correlations were performed to evaluate associations between diffusion metrics and cognitive performance. FDR correction was applied per bundle for all comparisons. RESULTS: After FDR correction, children with SeLECTS showed increased MD in the forceps minor, midbody of the corpus callosum, right corticospinal tract, right extreme capsule, and bilateral uncinate fasciculi. MD values in the affected WM segments showed negative correlations with performance and full-scale IQ, and the segments showing significant correlations overlapped with those showing significant group differences. CONCLUSIONS: SeLECTS is associated with MD-based microstructural alterations in superficial frontal, temporal, and parietal pathways, potentially indicating delayed white matter maturation.

title: Gαi2 promotes microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments to stabilise nascent axons in vivo.
abstract: Axon initiation is a critical step in the establishment of neuronal morphology. However, the mechanisms regulating stable axon initiation during embryonic development remain poorly understood. Here, using fixed-tissue super-resolution and high-resolution live-tissue imaging in the developing chick spinal cord, we reveal that stable axon initiation is characterised by microtubule-directed neurofilament accumulation in the emerging axon, and identify the multifunctional G-protein Gαi2 as a regulator of this process. Before axon initiation, microtubule network orientation shifts towards the site of the future axon where coiled Gαi2-associated neurofilaments accumulate asymmetrically before unfurling into the initiating axon behind microtubules. Crucially, Gαi2 is associated with neurofilaments and microtubules at their points of contact. Gαi2 depletion reduces engagement between these cytoskeletal networks and leads to impaired passage of neurofilaments into initiating axons and disrupted axon outgrowth, supporting a role for Gαi2 in regulating microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments in nascent axons. These findings advance mechanistic understanding of polarity establishment and provide insight into cytoskeletal regulation during axon formation.
authors: Higgs VE, Anwas D, Astapenka A, Toro-Tapia G, Das RM

title: Repurposed catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors tolcapone and entacapone preferentially suppress aggregation and seeding of P301 mutant tau in human neuronal models.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Pathogenic aggregation and propagation of seed-competent TAU assemblies drive tauopathies. MAPT P301 mutations accelerate aggregation and enhance seed competence, yet pharmacological strategies selectively targeting these pathogenic species remain limited. We investigated whether the clinically approved catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors tolcapone (TOL) and entacapone (ENT) preferentially modulate mutant TAU aggregation and seeding. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: TOL and ENT effects on TAU aggregation were evaluated via cell-free assays, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and in silico docking. Functional consequences of compound-modified fibrils were assessed in mutant TAU-expressing SH-SY5Y cells. Translational relevance was examined in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neurons exposed to pathogenic K18 fibrils, followed by post-seeding compound treatment. KEY RESULTS: Both compounds dose-dependently inhibited TAU aggregation, exhibiting greater potency, stronger SPR binding affinities, and more favourable computed interaction energies for P301S mutant versus wild-type TAU. Fibrils formed with TOL or ENT induced less downstream TAU oligomerization and phosphorylation in SH-SY5Y cells, with TOL showing superior protection. In hiPSC-derived neurons, post-seeding treatment with either compound decreased fibril-induced, sarkosyl-insoluble, TAU aggregation and phosphorylation without overt cytotoxicity. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: TOL and ENT preferentially reduced the aggregation and seeding of pathogenic P301 mutant TAU in the experimental models examined. These findings provide proof-of-concept support for mutation-focused pharmacological approaches and identify catechol scaffolds as starting points for developing more potent and safer TAU-directed compounds. Further studies are required to define the relevant molecular interactions, confirm the neuronal findings across additional hiPSC lines and determine whether effective CNS exposure can be achieved in vivo.

title: An integrated human forebrain organoid reveals microglia-mediated CD8+ T cell recruitment and neuroimmune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease pathology.
abstract: Genetic evidence implicates immune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the neuroimmune mechanisms operating in human tissue remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a modular human forebrain organoid platform that systematically integrates human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia and CD8+ T cells to reconstitute multicellular AD pathology. This system enables functional interrogation of both innate and adaptive immune components in a human-relevant context. Using this platform, we demonstrate that microglia mediate amyloid-β clearance and neuronal maturation but also drive inflammatory activation and recruit CD8+ T cells through CCL4/5 signaling via CCR1/5 and CXCR3, establishing a neuroinflammatory feedback loop. Pharmacological targeting of CCR5 or CXCR3 blocks T cell recruitment and modulates autophagy in a microglia-dependent manner. This modular organoid platform provides a versatile tool for dissecting neuron-immune interactions and enables cell-type-specific therapeutic screening in human neuroinflammatory disease models.

title: Astrocytic Ketogenesis Protects Central Nervous System Injury via CPT1A Stabilization and Epigenetic Regulation.
abstract: Following central nervous system (CNS) injury, reactive astrocytes proliferate and encapsulate the lesion to facilitate repair. However, the specific metabolic characteristics remain unknown. Here, through integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, we uncovered a subset of astrocytes that undergo enhanced lipid and ketone metabolic reprogramming following spinal cord injury (SCI). The ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB) inhibited autophagic degradation of carnitine-palmitoyltransferase-1A (CPT1A) via P300-mediated lysine β-hydroxybutyrylation (Kbhb). Astrocyte-specific deletion of Cpt1a led to impaired wound healing, reduced axonal sparing and worsened locomotor recovery after SCI, effects rescued by exogenous β-OHB. Mechanistically, ketogenesis promotes wound repair and lipid metabolic reprogramming, forming a positive feedback loop via H3K9bhb-dependent epigenetic remodeling in astrocytes after SCI. Furthermore, ketogenic diet (KD) promoted tissue repair across multiple CNS injury models. Clinically, elevated β-OHB levels were associated with better tissue preservation and functional recovery in SCI patients. Collectively, our findings underscore the critical role of astrocytic lipid metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming after CNS injury and identify KD as a promising therapeutic strategy.
authors: Pan D, Shu H, Gao R, Ren Y, Ye W, Ge X, Gu Y, Zhu Y, Wang X, Teng H
overview: Following central nervous system (CNS) injury, reactive astrocytes proliferate and encapsulate the lesion to facilitate repair.

title: Early lineage divergence segregates sensory and motor-associative identities in the thalamus.
abstract: The thalamus integrates sensory, motor and associative functions through distinct nuclei, yet the developmental principles driving their specification remain unclear. Here we generate a spatiotemporal single-cell multiomic and spatial transcriptomic atlas of the embryonic mouse thalamus, combined with barcoding-based lineage tracing. We identify two major glutamatergic lineages, sensory-related and motor-associative, each governed by different gene regulatory programs and temporal dynamics. These lineages arise from spatially and molecularly distinct progenitor domains, revealing an early segregation of functional identities. Within the sensory lineage, we resolve branching sensory trajectories leading to first-order visual and somatosensory neurons, both emerging from a shared higher-order-like state. Using in silico predictions and in vivo perturbation, we identify Sp9 as a key regulator of visual thalamic fate. Together, our findings define the molecular architecture and developmental trajectories that underpin thalamic modality specification, providing a framework to understand how functional circuits emerge in the mammalian brain.

overview: The thalamus integrates sensory, motor and associative functions through distinct nuclei, yet the developmental principles driving their specification remain unclear.

title: De novo variants in the essential splicing factor gene SRSF3 cause variable developmental phenotypes.
abstract: SRSF3 (SRp20), a member of the serine/arginine-rich protein family of splicing factors, plays a central role in constitutive and alternative splicing. The C-terminal arginine/serine-rich domain of SRSF3 undergoes dynamic phosphorylation cycles that regulate its subcellular localization, protein-protein interactions, and nuclear mRNA export while also indirectly modulating the RNA-binding capability. We report nine individuals with variable developmental phenotypes, including developmental delay and/or mild to moderate intellectual disability as the most consistent feature, and de novo SRSF3 variants. These variants comprise c.181G>C (p.Asp61His) and c.242C>G (p.Ser81Trp), affecting highly conserved residues within the RNA recognition motif, c.330_331del (p.Pro111Serfs∗20), c.402_403del (p.Arg137Ilefs∗16), c.477dup (p.Ser160Valfs∗3), and a recurrent nonsense variant c.445C>T (p.Arg149∗). For c.330_331del, nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) was predicted. Qualitative RT-PCR followed by Sanger sequencing and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of fibroblasts from this individual demonstrated NMD of SRSF3 transcripts containing the variant. However, overall SRSF3 mRNA and protein levels were comparable to control cells, suggestive of a compensatory mechanism acting in these cells. Comprehensive functional studies of ectopically expressed SRSF3Asp61His, SRSF3Ser81Trp, SRSF3Arg137Ilefs∗16, SRSF3Arg149∗, and SRSF3Ser160Valfs∗3 in HEK293T cells revealed reduced complex formation with polyadenylated RNA as well as intrinsic instability of C-terminally truncated variant proteins, correlating with decreased C-terminal phosphorylation. Complex formation with the nuclear export proteins YTHDC1 and NXF1 was reduced for SRSF3Arg137Ilefs∗16 and SRSF3Arg149∗ and increased for SRSF3Ser81Trp. Additionally, nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, assessed in HeLa cells, was reduced for the C-terminally truncated SRSF3 variant proteins. Together, our data demonstrate distinct functional defects for the disease-associated SRSF3 variants, which may underlie phenotypic variability in affected individuals.

title: Thalamic PDK-PDHA1 Signaling is Associated with Opioid-Induced Loss-of-Righting-Reflex Sensitivity: Evidence from Phosphoproteomic Profiling and PDK Pathway Intervention.
abstract: Opioids are widely used in clinical sedation and anesthesia, but the downstream phosphorylation events associated with opioid-induced reductions in arousal remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated whether thalamic phosphoproteomic remodeling and the pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK)-pyruvate dehydrogenase E1 alpha subunit (PDHA1) pathway are associated with opioid-induced loss of righting reflex (LORR) in rats. Phosphoproteomic profiling of rat thalamic tissues after treatment with fentanyl, FENT-001 (a synthetic fentanyl analog), and other sedative and anesthetic agents revealed broad changes in thalamic phosphopeptide abundance.Differentially phosphorylated proteins were enriched in neuronal projections, synapses, cytoskeletal organization and synaptic transmission. PDHA1 was identified as a significantly differentially phosphorylated protein and was further examined by Western blotting. Fentanyl and 3-methylfentanyl altered phosphorylation at multiple PDHA1 sites. Pharmacological inhibition of PDKs with dichloroacetate reduced PDHA1 Ser293 phosphorylation in cultured cortical neurons and produced numerical increases in the estimated ED50 values for fentanyl- and 3-methylfentanyl-induced LORR. These changes were consistent with a trend toward reduced LORR sensitivity. Conversely, CM-targeted overexpression of PDK2 or PDK4 shifted the fitted fentanyl-induced LORR dose-response curves to the left relative to the Vector control, with a larger numerical reduction in ED50 following PDK2 overexpression.These findings suggest that opioid treatment remodels the thalamic phosphoproteome and that the PDK-PDHA1 phosphorylation pathway is functionally associated with opioid-induced LORR sensitivity.

title: Integration of polygenic risk with single cell methylation data using met-scDRS.
abstract: MOTIVATION: Although large scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many risk variants for psychiatric traits their functional implication remain largely unknown. One potential mechanism for their risk is through cellular context-dependent epigenetics such as methylation. Previous methodologies have focused on integrating GWAS with single cell transcriptomics, which allowed identification of within-cell-type heterogeneity in disease risk association. We extended this framework to provide a method called met-scDRS that integrates GWAS with single cell epigenomics and investigates how psychiatric disease risk can manifest through methylomics at single cell resolution. RESULTS: We propose an approach that integrates single cell methylomes with disease associated genes identified from GWAS at single-cell resolution. We found our method to be well calibrated and powered in different scenarios. We then analyzed a publicly available single cell methylome dataset of the human brain for 75 different traits and generated disease relevance scores for each cell for each trait. We find high brain specificity with major cell type enrichments congruent with known findings. We identify within-cell-type heterogeneity for psychiatric disease risk along the brain spatial axis as well as subpopulations that are differentially associated with diseases. Finally, we showed that genes with high correlation between methylation levels and disease relevance scores to be highly enriched in specific functional pathways such as synaptic formation and transmission. AVAILABILITY: met-scDRS is freely available in GitHub as a python package under MIT license: https://github.com/bogdanlab/met-scDRS. Source code is also available from Zenodo with DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21841506. All dataset used in this work are publicly available. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.
authors: Li X, Shi Z, Hou K, Eyring KW, Liu C, Heffel MG, Luo C, Geschwind DH, Pasaniuc B
overview: MOTIVATION: Although large scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many risk variants for psychiatric traits their functional implication remain largely unknown.

title: Subdiffraction fluorescence lifetime imaging with Flipper-TR.
abstract: The combination of stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy with fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) offers a powerful route to functional super-resolution imaging, but remains technically challenging for lifetime-based sensing because of the complex interplay between stimulated emission, photon budget, and accurate lifetime quantification. In this technical note, we evaluate and optimize STED-FLIM for nanoscale mapping of bacterial membrane mechanics using the mechanosensitive probe Flipper-TR. This probe is particularly demanding for STED-FLIM because it exhibits a biexponential fluorescence decay, with only the long lifetime reporting on membrane mechanical properties. Using liveBacillus subtiliscells, we establish an acquisition and analysis workflow that combines optimized imaging conditions with tail fitting to minimize distortions introduced by the depletion pulse. Under these conditions, STED imaging achieved a more than twofold improvement in spatial resolution compared with confocal microscopy, while maintaining sufficient photon counts for robust lifetime estimation. Finally, we discuss the trade-offs between spatial resolution and photon budget and provide practical recommendations for implementing STED-FLIM with environmentally sensitive probes. These results extend the application of Flipper-TR to functional super-resolution microscopy and provide a framework for robust STED-FLIM measurements of membrane nanomechanics and other fluorescence lifetime-based sensing applications.

title: Investigating Structural Heterogeneities of Amyloid Aggregates with Spatially Resolved Infrared Spectroscopy.
abstract: The aggregation of proteins into fibrillar amyloids is central to the pathology of neurodegenerative disorders. However, the relationship between the structure of amyloid aggregates and disease progression remains incompletely understood, in part because amyloid systems are intrinsically heterogeneous: structurally distinct species coexist at every stage of aggregation, and conventional ensemble-averaged methods cannot always resolve them. This Account describes how infrared spectroscopy can be coupled to different imaging modalities to resolve this heterogeneity at multiple length scales: from single-aggregate level to amyloid species in diseased brain tissues. Our findings demonstrate that (i) early stage tau fibrils exhibit pronounced structural polymorphism without morphological differences, converging to a single dominant conformation upon maturation that unexpectedly includes antiparallel β-sheet structure; (ii) Aβ42 oligomeric heterogeneity propagates through protofibrils into fibrils, where structurally distinct domains coexist along a single fibril, demonstrating that amyloid fibrils can deviate significantly from the canonical parallel cross-β architecture; (iii) Aβ(16-22) fibrils undergo a parallel-to-antiparallel β-sheet transition during maturation through disordered intermediates without morphological change, providing direct evidence of spontaneous structural reorganization in fibrillar species. Beyond single-protein systems, (iv) Aβ42 forms structurally distinct mixed polymorphs when aggregated with sequentially or structurally heterotypic seeds and when coaggregated with α-synuclein, establishing heterotypic interactions as an underappreciated source of aberrant aggregate structures; (v) coaggregation of Aβ with the islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) from the monomeric state produces a unique heterotypic polymorph in which both peptides adopt non-native structures, whereas cross-seeding with preformed IAPP fibrils yields predominantly homotypic Aβ aggregates, demonstrating that conformational flexibility at the monomeric stage is required for heterotypic fibril formation. These molecular-level findings are complemented by tissue-scale evidence: (vi) discrete frequency IR imaging reveals that amyloid plaques in AD brain exhibit chemical and structural heterogeneities not reflected in morphology, consistent with in vitro observations; and (vii) optical photothermal infrared (O-PTIR) spectroscopic imaging of vascular amyloid deposits in cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) reveals a disease-stage-dependent increase in antiparallel β-sheet content that correlates specifically with colocalized lipids, recapitulated in vitro by coaggregating Aβ40 with lipid extracts. Collectively, these findings support the view that structural heterogeneity is not merely an artifact of in vitro conditions but a property that can persist in human brain tissues and illustrate how spatially resolved IR spectroscopy can complement cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and solid-state NMR in the study of amyloid pathology.

overview: The aggregation of proteins into fibrillar amyloids is central to the pathology of neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Targeting the Calcium-mtDNA-cGAS-STING Signaling Nexus: A Novel Redox Mechanism for Nimodipine's Neuroprotection in Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) induces severe secondary injury where molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates the involvement of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling pathway in this process and evaluates the neuroprotective effect of the L-type calcium channel blocker nimodipine, focusing on calcium homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory signaling. METHODS: Using primary neuronal and mouse TBI models, we assessed outcomes via fluorescent calcium imaging, JC-1 staining, Western blot, quantitative PCR (qPCR)/reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and behavioral tests. Nimodipine was applied to inhibit L-type channels, specifically testing its role in reducing mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release, blocking cGAS-STING activation, and suppressing neuroinflammation. RESULTS: TBI markedly activated the cGAS-STING pathway, increasing pro-inflammatory factors and apoptosis. In the cellular oxygen-glucose deprivation model, calcium overload was directly observed by Fluo-4 AM staining and was associated with subsequent mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening and mtDNA release, identifying this process as a key upstream event for cGAS-STING activation. Nimodipine inhibited intracellular calcium overload, reduced mitochondrial injury and mtDNA release, and consequently suppressed cGAS-STING pathway activation. Both in vivo and in vitro experiments showed dose-dependent decreases in pro-inflammatory factors, along with improved neurological function and attenuated brain tissue pathology. CONCLUSION: Nimodipine attenuates secondary neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis after TBI by inhibiting calcium influx, decreasing mtDNA release, and suppressing cGAS-STING signaling. These results suggest that the Ca2+-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis contributes to TBI pathology and that nimodipine may serve as a potential multitarget therapy. Antioxid. Redox Signal. 00, 000-000.

title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-hour continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

title: cAMP signaling promotes acute lysosome biogenesis through TFEB nuclear import-export dynamics.
abstract: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling is a major stimulus for lipid and glucose catabolism, yet catabolic processes like these can also coordinate with lysosome-dependent degradation. However, the impact of cAMP signaling on lysosomal dynamics remains unclear. Transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, is regulated by stimulus-dependent nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling through a variety of phosphorylation events. Here, we find that elevating intracellular cAMP with forskolin and IBMX induces rapid nuclear import of TFEB-GFP within 30 minutes and coincides with a transient upregulation of TFEB target lysosome genes. By 8 hours, TFEB returns to the cytoplasm, accompanied by transcriptional downregulation. Inhibition of cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) using H89 did not block nuclear import but unexpectedly caused sustained nuclear accumulation, indicating that PKA promotes TFEB nuclear export. Consistent with this, phosphoproteomic profiling revealed increased phosphorylation of a PKA-consensus motif (RRxS) during the export phase. These findings suggest that cAMP-PKA signaling plays a novel role in temporally "tuning" lysosomal gene expression by regulating TFEB nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling.

title: Beyond Alzheimer's story: How an engineered molecule gained an endogenous essence.
abstract: A hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is extra-neuronal protein aggregates formed mainly by the amyloid-β peptide (Aβ), that are deposited inside the brain as amyloid plaques. The formation of amyloid plaques requires participation of zinc ions. The 11-Glu-Val-His-His-14 region of Aβ is critical for interaction between Aβ and zinc ions. The engineered peptide Ac-His-Ala-Glu-Glu-NH2 (HAEE) acts as competitive inhibitor of such interactions and suppresses formation of Aβ aggregates in animal models of AD. We sought to develop a reliable method for studying the behavior of the synthetic HAEE peptide in the human blood in preparation for clinical trials of this peptide as a potential anti-amyloid drug for AD. The analytical method to monitor HAEE concentration in blood plasma combines separation by high-performance liquid chromatography and registration on a mass detector of the parent quasi-molecular ion and fragment ions. We discover that HAEE peptide represents a normal endogenous component of human blood plasma. Moreover, the HAEE level has been significantly reduced in patients with a clinical diagnosis of AD (n = 200) as compared with the control participants with no clinical diagnosis of cognitive impairment (n = 150). Deficiency of endogenous HAEE may be considered as a potential blood-based biomarker in the diagnosis of AD, while exogenous synthetic HAEE may serve as a drug in AD-modifying therapy.

title: Dysregulated cholesterol trafficking through ABCA1 drives neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Although brain cholesterol dysregulation is implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), targeting cholesterol synthesis has shown limited efficacy. Here we identify ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) as a critical regulator of cholesterol homeostasis in PD. We show that ABCA1 expression is elevated in the substantia nigra of postmortem PD brains and in a PD mouse model, with regional analyses revealing preferential alterations in nigral and striatal circuits. Mechanistically, astrocytic ABCA1 drives excessive cholesterol efflux in mice, promoting neuronal cholesterol overload. In neurons, ABCA1 localizes to lysosomes, where it facilitates cholesterol import, leading to cholesterol accumulation, autophagy impairment and α-synuclein pathology. Genetic silencing of Abca1 in either astrocytes or dopaminergic neurons attenuates neurodegeneration and behavioral deficits in vivo. Furthermore, we identify magnesium citrate as an ABCA1 inhibitor and show that it reduces dopaminergic neuronal loss in a PD mouse model. Our findings identify an ABCA1-dependent cholesterol pathway underlying PD pathogenesis and support ABCA1 inhibition as a potential disease-modifying strategy.

title: Elastin-derived peptide VGVAPG induces redox-associated pro-inflammatory activation and early disease-associated microglia (DAM) molecular profile in a human microglia-neuron in vitro model involving NEU1/TLR4-related signaling.
abstract: The elastin-derived hexapeptide Val-Gly-Val-Ala-Pro-Gly (VGVAPG) exhibits well-documented biological activity; however, its role in brain inflammation remains insufficiently characterized. This is an important issue, as VGVAPG levels increase with age and have been implicated in processes contributing to neurodegeneration. The present study aimed to evaluate the ability of aging-related VGVAPG to activate human microglial (HMC3) cells in vitro and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Our results demonstrated no cytotoxic effect of VGVAPG. However, further analyses revealed NF-κB nuclear translocation, elevated ROS and •NO production, enhanced iNOS, and accumulation of NLRP3-containing vesicles in the cytoplasm, consistent with the peptide's pro-inflammatory potential. Additionally, activation of stress- and inflammation-related signaling pathways involving p38-MAPK, JNKs, and ERK1/2 was observed, accompanied by upregulation of NFKB1, IL1B, and TNFα mRNA. Using a transwell co-culture model of HMC3 and cholinergic-like neurons (differentiated SH-SY5Y), we observed potential DAMP-associated molecular changes involving HMGB1 and APP. Additionally, NEU1 siRNA-mediated knockdown in HMC3 cells, together with the observed NEU1/TLR4 colocalization, raises the possibility that NEU1 and TLR4 may be involved in the effects induced by VGVAPG. Moreover, VGVAPG induced alterations in early disease-associated microglia (DAM)-related protein profiles, including β2M, ITGAX, and ICAM1. Collectively, these findings identify VGVAPG as a candidate pro-neuroinflammatory matrikine in vitro and provide associative evidence for selected redox, NEU1-, TLR4-related, and early DAM-associated molecular changes. Further investigations employing advanced in vivo and translational models are warranted to validate these observations and to clarify the pathophysiological role of VGVAPG in the progression of neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Carbon-12 and Gamma-Rays Combined Irradiation Ameliorates Behavioral and Biochemical Alterations in Tau P301S Homozygous Transgenic Mice.
abstract: No effective treatments currently exist for tauopathies. Given emerging evidence that moderate-dose ionizing radiation (IR) may exert neuroreparative effects in neurodegeneration, we investigated the impact of combined IR exposure on disease progression in the Tau P301S mouse model. Tau P301S mice received combined gamma-ray (0.24 Gy) and carbon-12 nuclei (0.18 Gy, 400 MeV/n) irradiation at the presymptomatic stage. Following longitudinal behavioral testing until the terminal stage, post-mortem brains were analyzed via RT-qPCR, ELISA, and HPLC to assess gene expression, protein levels, and monoamine quantification. At the symptomatic stage, Tau+R mice showed normalized endurance, fear-dependent memory, and disinhibition-like behavior, reaching wild-type levels. At the terminal stage, Tau+R mice demonstrated significantly superior balance, coordination, and grip strength compared to untreated Tau P301S mice. These benefits correlated with restored striatal serotonin and a 76% reduction in cerebellar tau protein (transcription-independent). Furthermore, IR normalized Gsk3b expression in the hippocampus and cerebellum, and Trem2 in the cerebellum, to WT levels. Notably, IR up-regulated cerebellar Iba1 by 31% and 86% compared to WT and Tau mice, respectively. Combined radiotherapy not only alleviates behavioral symptoms but also modulates key neurochemical parameters. These findings demonstrate robust symptomatic improvements and suggest a potential neuroprotective capacity of combined radiotherapy in a mouse model of severe tauopathy.

title: Cucurbituril-modulated NIR emission and two-photon mitochondrial imaging of an acridine derivative.
abstract: Host-guest assemblies of an acridine dye with cucurbit[7]uril and cucurbit[8]uril give distinct NIR emissions at 674 and 708 nm, respectively. Both exhibit efficient two-photon absorption near 925 nm and successfully enable single- and two-photon mitochondrial imaging in live A549 cells.

title: Autism: epidemiology, genetics, molecular mechanisms, clinical features, diagnosis, and management.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Global prevalence has risen steadily, yet reported rates vary markedly across regions and populations. These discrepancies reflect inequities in diagnostic access and screening capacity rather than true differences in incidence. This review integrates recent advances across the full ASD research spectrum. We first examine global epidemiological patterns and demographic disparities. We then dissect the genetic architecture of ASD, including rare and common variants, copy number variations, and gene-environment interactions that disrupt prenatal and early postnatal brain development. At the molecular level, diverse risk factors converge on shared neurodevelopmental mechanisms. These include synaptic dysfunction, dysregulated signaling through mTOR, Ras-ERK-MAPK, Wnt and Notch pathways, impaired neurogenesis, chronic neuroimmune inflammation, and excitatory-inhibitory imbalance. We also discuss how these mechanisms manifest in core clinical features, including social deficits, repetitive behaviors, and sensory abnormalities. We summarize current diagnostic standards and their limitations. Cross-species animal models, from Drosophila to non-human primates, are evaluated for their essential roles in mechanistic validation and therapeutic screening. Finally, we assess clinical management strategies, ranging from behavioral and educational interventions to pharmacological and supportive services. By tracing a continuous path from risk factors at the population level through molecular pathophysiology to interventions guided by mechanism, this review offers an integrative synthesis that connects basic discovery to clinical translation. We further discuss how multi-omics and artificial intelligence may advance precise diagnosis rooted in mechanism and personalized treatment.

title: Bidirectional Regulatory Mechanisms of T cell-microglia Interactions in Cerebral Ischemic Disease: Molecular Crosstalk, Experimental Techniques and Therapeutic Implications.
abstract: Cerebral ischemic diseases, such as ischemic stroke (IS) and vascular dementia (VaD), are major causes of neurological disability and mortality. Neuroinflammation acts as a pivotal driver of secondary brain injury, mediated by intricate bidirectional interactions between peripheral T cells and central nervous system (CNS)-resident microglia. This review delineates the molecular mechanisms underlying T cell-microglia crosstalk in cerebral ischemia, emphasizing their dual roles in exacerbating neurotoxicity and promoting repair. Direct interactions involve antigen presentation via MHC-TCR engagement and co-stimulatory checkpoints (e.g., CD80/CD86-CD28, PD-L1-PD-1), which regulate T cell activation and microglial polarization. Direct signaling through cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-17, IL-10) further modulates microglial phenotypes: Th1/Th17 cells drive pro-inflammatory M1 polarization via STAT1/NF-κB pathways, while Tregs/Th2 cells induce anti-inflammatory M2 states through STAT6/SMAD signaling. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell omics reveal spatiotemporal dynamics of these interactions, identifying STAT1/STAT6 imbalance as a critical determinant of neuroinflammatory outcomes. Advanced methodologies, including two-photon intravital microscopy and microfluidic blood-brain barrier (BBB) models, enable real-time visualization of immune cell trafficking and synaptic communication. Therapeutically, targeting immune checkpoints (CTLA-4, PD-1) or cytokine pathways (e.g., IL-4 mimetics) shows promise in recalibrating neuroimmune responses. However, challenges such as blood-brain barrier impermeability to biologics and interspecies immune heterogeneity necessitate innovative delivery strategies. This review integrates molecular, cellular, and technological insights to propose a framework for precision immunomodulation. By elucidating context-dependent signaling nodes and leveraging emerging tools, the study underscores the potential of harnessing T cell-microglia crosstalk to mitigate neuroinflammation and enhance neural repair, offering transformative avenues for stroke and dementia therapy.

title: The molecular footprint of valproic acid in human hippocampal organoid.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a multifaceted neurodevelopmental condition characterized by neuroinflammation, and disruption in neuronal development. Valproic acid (VPA) is a known environmental risk factor for ASD. Induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs IMR90-4)-derived human hippocampal organoids (hHOs) at 60 days of development were used to investigate VPA-induced changes in mRNA and microRNA (miRNA) profiles. The molecular effects of VPA on hHOs were deciphered by meaningfully integrating the ability of miRNA to regulate expression of their predicted mRNA targets crucial to altering neuroinflammatory pathways. Molecular footprint can be defined as the VPA-induced changes to the miRNA profile resulting in coordinated post-transcriptional (mRNA) regulation of neuronal and inflammatory pathways associated with ASD. Based on the results, the molecular footprint of VPA in hHOs was generated for the first time. These findings highlight the contribution of miRNA-mediated regulatory mRNA networks to VPA-induced neuroinflammation-associated with ASD in hHOs.

title: Absent Septum Pellucidum Without Polymicrogyria or Seizures in TCP1-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder.
abstract: T-complex protein 1 (TCP1) encodes the TCP1α subunit, one of eight subunits of the chaperonin containing TCP1 ring complex (TRiC). Heterozygous TCP1 variants cause autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by developmental delay or intellectual disability, seizures, pyramidal or cerebellar signs, and brain malformations, particularly polymicrogyria. However, the reported clinical spectrum remains limited. We report a 4-year-old girl with global developmental delay, speech and motor delay, behavioral dysregulation, microcephaly, hypotonia with core weakness, and a previously unreported heterozygous likely pathogenic TCP1 variant, c.1392delT (p.A465Qfs*3). This frameshift variant is located in exon 11, truncates the final 16.5% of the protein, is predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay, and is absent from gnomAD. Biological parental testing was unavailable, precluding determination of variant inheritance. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated an absent septum pellucidum with mild bilateral frontal sulcation/gyration asymmetry without polymicrogyria; the optic nerves and pituitary were normal. No seizures were documented through age 4 years. Additional findings included bicuspid aortic valve with mild aortic insufficiency, asthma, severe eczema/atopy, and multiple food allergies. This case suggests that the molecular and neuroimaging spectrum of TCP1-related neurodevelopmental disorder may be broader than previously recognized; however, a causal association between TCP1 and absent septum pellucidum cannot be established from a single case. The relationship of the cardiac and atopic findings to TCP1 remains uncertain. Additional cases and functional studies are needed to clarify genotype-phenotype relationships.

title: A pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts hippocampal synapse maturation and homeostasis.
abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for activity-dependent synapse maturation and circuit development. De novo missense mutations in AMPAR subunits are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet how these variants disrupt neuronal function remains unclear. Here, we examine a recurrent pathogenic mutation in the GluA1 subunit (GRIA1 p.A636T) that alters AMPAR function and is associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using GluA1A636T knock-in mice of either sex, we identify impairments in hippocampal-dependent learning and working memory. Quantitative proteomics combined with bulk RNA-seq revealed age-dependent molecular remodeling in mutant hippocampus. Synaptic protein alterations were present in juvenile and adult mice, whereas a pronounced upregulation of mitochondrial and glial-associated proteins emerged more strongly in adulthood. Transcriptomic analyses showed partial concordance and highlighted divergence between RNA and protein regulation. Consistent with these molecular changes, there were increases in markers of oxidative stress in juvenile and adult mutant animals, whereas altered mitochondria morphology emerged selectively in adult mutants. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated reduced basal excitatory transmission, persistence of silent synapses in adulthood and exaggerated activity-dependent synaptic potentiation, which were associated with reduced spine size consistent with impaired synapse maturation. Together, these findings indicate that a pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts developmental synapse maturation with secondary metabolic adaptations emerging over time.Significance Statement Mutations in genes encoding AMPA-type glutamate receptors are increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism and intellectual disability. However, how these mutations disrupt brain function and development remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model carrying a recurrent disease-associated mutation in the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit, we show that the presence of this mutant subunit protein impairs the normal maturation of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus. Mutant mice retain immature "silent" synapses into adulthood, exhibit abnormal synaptic plasticity, reduced spine size, and deficits in learning and memory. Molecular analyses reveal age-dependent remodeling of synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, suggesting that metabolic changes arise secondary to disrupted synapse development. These findings clarify how pathogenic AMPA receptor variants alter brain function over time.

title: Validating gene-brain-behavior associations in autism: A replication study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism is characterized by heterogeneity in clinical characteristics, neuroimaging and genetic profiles. To elucidate the multi-level heterogeneity, Buch et al. (2023) identified biologically meaningful subgroups in Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE). However, ABIDE contains non-biological sources of variability due to retrospectively aligned site protocols. To separate biological from site-related variability and test the robustness of these subgroups, we assessed how well their findings replicate in a deeply phenotyped, prospectively collected autism dataset (EU-AIMS LEAP). METHODS: We included 270 autistic (7.5-30.3 years; 73% male) and 216 non-autistic participants (6.9-31 years; 63.4% male) from LEAP. Regularized canonical correlation analysis (RCCA) was conducted between functional connectivity and three clinical measures (verbal IQ [VIQ], and Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule-2 [ADOS-2] social affect [SA] and restricted/repetitive behavior [RRB]). Next, subgroups identified by hierarchical clustering based on canonical variates were characterized by behavior, functional connectivity patterns and gene enrichment analyses. RESULTS: Three of four autistic subgroups showed behavioral profiles consistent with the original study. Three subgroups shared stronger thalamocortical connectivity, while all four displayed distinct connectivity involving default mode network (DMN), salience (SN), visual and somatomotor networks. These subgroup-specific connectivity patterns were further linked to autism-associated and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related gene sets. Across preprocessing pipelines, subgroup assignments were partially preserved. Subgroup2 (globally affected behaviors) and Subgroup4 (less social difficulty, but more restricted behavior) retained more consistent behavioral profiles and connectivity alterations, whereas Subgroup1 and Subgroup3 were more sensitive to the precise preprocessing steps. CONCLUSIONS: These four subgroups showed partly consistent behavioral profiles, connectivity alterations and genetic patterns, extending our understanding of the multi-level heterogeneity of autism.

title: Neurobehavioral Profiles and Clinical Consequences of MYT1L-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder: Insights From the Brain Gene Registry.
abstract: MYT1L-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder (MYT1L-NDD) is a rare autosomal dominant syndrome characterized by intellectual disability, global developmental delay, autism, and obesity. Despite growing recognition, prospective and systematic clinical phenotyping remains limited. Here, we present an exploratory analysis of data from 25 individuals with MYT1L-NDD enrolled in the Brain Gene Registry (BGR), a national platform integrating genetic, neurobehavioral, and clinical data. Neurobehavioral assessments were conducted using the Rapid Neurobehavioral Assessment Protocol (RNAP), including virtual adaptations of the Shipley, Developmental Profile-4, ASEBA Child Behavior Checklist, and Vineland-3. Diagnostic and medication data were extracted from structured electronic health records (EHR). MYT1L-NDD participants were compared to the broader BGR cohort. MYT1L-NDD participants exhibited pronounced impairments in nonverbal cognition and adaptive functioning, particularly in motor tasks, communication, and daily living skills. Behavioral assessments revealed elevated rates of autism symptoms, ADHD symptoms, behavioral conduct problems, oppositional defiance, and anxiety. EHR diagnosis data were available for 10 MYT1L-NDD participants. It showed frequent diagnoses of developmental delays, speech and language disorders, intellectual disability, gastrointestinal problems, and obesity. Medication data on five participants indicated common prescription of alpha-2 adrenergic agonists and laxatives. This study provides the first prospective, multi-source characterization of MYT1L-NDD. Findings expand our understanding of MYT1L-NDD phenotypes in a quantitative and systematic manner and support the value of registry-based approaches for understanding rare neurodevelopmental disorders. Larger, longitudinal, age-stratified studies are needed to further define MYT1L-NDD natural history and inform clinical care.

title: Metformin partially modulates cisplatin-induced neuronal senescence but does not prevent rat peripheral sensory hypersensitivity.
abstract: Therapy-induced senescence (TIS) is recognized as a contributor to chemotherapy-associated adverse effects, including neurotoxicity. While senolytics have shown promise in alleviating chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), their clinical translation might be hindered by unfavorable safety profiles, shifting interest toward less toxic senomorphics. We investigated the senomorphic potential of metformin (Met) in counteracting cisplatin (Cis)-induced senescence using both an in vitro model of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons (iPSC-MNs) and an in vivo rat model of CIPN. Exposure of iPSC-MNs to Cis induced hallmark features of senescence, including increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity and upregulation of senescence-associated markers, as confirmed by immunofluorescence (increased p16INK4a and decreased Lamin B1) and qPCR (CDKN2A, CDKN1A, CXCL8 upregulation) analyses. While Met did not significantly reduce SA-β-gal activity or restore cell viability, it attenuated the expression of key senescence-associated transcripts, including CDKN2A and components of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) such as CXCL8, indicating partial senomorphic activity. In vivo, Cis administered in two cycles (cumulative dose: 23 mg/kg) elicited mechanical allodynia and thermal hyperalgesia in Sprague-Dawley rats. Analysis of dorsal root ganglia (DRG) on day 8 post-treatment revealed strong SA-β-gal staining and increased expression of cdkn1a, cdkn2a, and SASP mediators (Il6). Met pretreatment reversed the upregulation of cdkn1a, cdkn2a, and Il6, but did not alleviate the sensory deficits induced by Cis. Our findings support a partial senomorphic activity of Met both in vitro and in vivo yet demonstrate its limited efficacy in functionally mitigating CIPN.

title: Identification of Succinylation-Related Transcriptional Signatures in Alzheimer's Disease: Integrated Bioinformatics Analysis and Clinical Validation.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder involving mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, proteostasis imbalance, and immune-inflammatory alterations. Protein succinylation is closely linked to mitochondrial metabolic status, but peripheral blood transcriptomic signatures related to succinylation in AD remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to identify peripheral blood transcriptional candidate biomarkers associated with a predefined succinylation-related gene set in AD. The GSE63061 dataset was used as the discovery cohort, and GSE63060 served as an external validation cohort. Differential expression analysis, ssGSEA-derived succinylation scoring, and WGCNA were integrated with a predefined succinylation-related gene set. Candidate biomarkers were then refined through four feature selection approaches: LASSO, random forest, SVM-RFE, and Boruta, and their discriminatory performance was evaluated by ROC analysis, nomogram construction, calibration analysis, decision curve analysis, and SHAP analysis. Functional enrichment, GSVA/GSEA, GeneMANIA, immune-cell signature analysis, and single-cell analyses were used to explore biological relevance and cellular distribution. qRT-PCR was performed using peripheral blood-derived PBMC samples for experimental validation. Five genes, NDUFA1, NDUFS5, RPS27A, AIF1, and PRDX1, were identified as candidate biomarkers associated with a succinylation-related transcriptional signature in AD. These genes were mainly involved in mitochondrial complex I activity, oxidative phosphorylation, ribosomal function, protein homeostasis, redox balance, and immune inflammation. Immune-cell signatures and single-cell analyses further suggested that the signature was associated with T cells, B cells, NK cells, and monocytes/macrophages. qRT-PCR confirmed significant downregulation of all five genes in AD PBMC samples (P < 0.05). These findings suggest that peripheral blood transcriptional signatures associated with succinylation-related genes may provide candidate biomarkers and hypothesis-generating clues for AD.

overview: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder involving mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, proteostasis imbalance, and immune-inflammatory alterations.
main: qRT-PCR was performed using peripheral blood-derived PBMC samples for experimental validation.

title: Exploratory chromosome 14-focused transcriptomic profiling of PSEN1-associated familial Alzheimer's disease across brain regions.
abstract: Familial Alzheimer's disease (FAD) is an inherited form of early-onset Alzheimer's disease associated with pathogenic variants in presenilin 1 (PSEN1). To explore chromosome 14-associated transcriptional patterns in FAD across anatomically distinct brain regions, publicly available RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) datasets from frontal cortex, temporal cortex, and whole-brain samples were analyzed. Because one FAD sample and one control sample were available for each brain region, expression differences were evaluated descriptively using observed log₂ fold-change values rather than conventional inferential differential-expression statistics. Functional annotation and protein-protein interaction analyses were subsequently used to provide biological context for the observed expression patterns. Distinct regional expression patterns were observed within the chromosome 14-focused dataset. Higher expression was observed for representative genes including FITM1, IFI27, AHSA1, and NFKBIA in the frontal cortex, and DHRS4L2, ESR2, GPR65, EFCAB11, and HOMEZ in the temporal cortex. The observed expression patterns were associated with inflammatory, cellular stress, metabolic, receptor-mediated, proteostatic, and neuronal signaling-related functions. Network analysis was used to contextualize these expression patterns rather than to infer causal regulatory relationships. Five representative proteins-NFKBIA, ESR2, GPR65, AHSA1, and IFI27-were further examined structural information to provide structural context for selected transcriptomic observations. Given the absence of biological replication and the chromosome 14-focused design, these findings should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Independent replicated cohorts and complementary transcriptomic, proteomic, and functional studies are required to determine the reproducibility and biological relevance of the observed patterns.

title: Loss of CRMP4 in astrocytes causes reduced scar formation and functional recovery of motor function after spinal cord injury.
abstract: Reactive astrocytes play a central role in shaping the post-injury microenvironment after spinal cord injury (SCI), yet the molecular mechanisms governing their proliferative expansion and contribution to scar architecture remain incompletely defined. Conditional deletion of CRMP4 in astrocytes significantly reduced astrocyte proliferation, altered scar organization, and attenuated the inflammatory milieu surrounding the lesion, including reduced microglial activation. These changes were accompanied by significantly improved locomotor recovery, as assessed by the Basso Mouse Scale (BMS) locomotor rating scale, indicating enhanced functional restoration after SCI. Our findings suggest that CRMP4 promotes the expansion of reactive astrocyte subsets that shape the inhibitory niche surrounding the lesion core, thereby restricting axonal regeneration and limiting functional recovery after SCI. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis of a public dataset revealed that Crmp4 expression is enriched in proliferative, progenitor-like astrocyte subpopulations that contribute to scar formation, including subclusters corresponding to the G2/M phases of the cell cycle. Together, this study identifies astrocytic CRMP4 as a key molecular determinant of reactive astrocyte dynamics and scar architecture after SCI, providing new insight into cell-type-specific regulation of glial responses in central nervous system injury.

title: Evaluation of Methylmercury-Induced Motor Dysfunction and Proteomic Analysis of Cerebrospinal Fluid in Common Marmosets (Callithrix jacchus).
abstract: Methylmercury (MeHg) poisoning can lead to Minamata disease, often manifesting as motor dysfunction. We aimed to establish a quantitative evaluation method for MeHg exposure-associated motor dysfunction in the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus). Three male marmosets were orally administered MeHg (1.5 mg Hg/kg/day) for 2 weeks, followed by a 2-week non-treatment period; three control marmosets received vehicle. Walking and spontaneous behavior were recorded weekly. After marking body segments, bounding gait videos were analyzed to assess locomotion speed, hip joint position, knee angle, dorsal neck-to-torso angle, and spontaneous behavior. In Hg-1 (MeHg-exposed marmoset with earliest symptom onset), locomotion speed and stride length decreased, while stride time increased. In Hg-2 (second marmoset to exhibit symptom onset), hip joint position and knee angle initially showed relatively normal fluctuations during bounding gait. However, their lower limits decreased following MeHg administration, and the dorsal neck-to-torso angle shifted from negative to positive. Spontaneous activity of Hg-1 and Hg-2 significantly decreased after MeHg administration. These results indicate that MeHg exposure-associated motor dysfunction in marmosets can be detected using our method, with particularly prominent lower-limb abnormalities. Furthermore, cerebrospinal fluid proteomic profiling revealed coordinated disruptions converging on three pathological axes-neuronal injury and neuroprotective responses, neuronal metabolic failure and cytosolic enzyme leakage, and impaired transport and homeostatic regulation-identifying nine proteins as candidate biomarkers. Proteomic alterations were consistent with the observed neuronal injury, neuroinflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and impaired homeostatic regulation in affected motor pathways. These findings establish the marmoset as a translational primate model for neurotoxicological assessments and biomarker discovery.

title: Single-cell atlas of neuroma-induced DRG remodeling reveals intervention-specific glial and immune programs.
abstract: Peripheral nerve injury caused by cut, crush, or excessive stretch can lead to disordered regeneration and painful neuroma formation. Regrowing axons may terminate in a swollen, hypersensitive nerve stump, producing pain that can outweigh sensory or motor deficits. Despite the frequency of neuromas, treatment outcomes remain inconsistent, and the mechanisms that initiate and sustain neuroma-associated pain are poorly understood. A proximal nerve crush performed upstream of a neuroma or transection may reshape axonal growth and interrupt retrograde injury signaling, potentially promoting a regenerative, pain-resolving state. However, its long-term effects on dorsal root ganglion (DRG) programs remain unclear. Here, we use single-cell RNA sequencing to build an atlas of DRG remodeling after neuroma-forming injury and compare it with two interventions: proximal nerve crush and nerve resection. By resolving transcriptional responses across sensory neurons, satellite glial cells, Schwann cells, and macrophages, we identify intervention-specific glial, neuronal, and immune programs that distinguish regenerative from persistent injury-associated states and nominate pathways that may guide mechanism-based therapies for painful neuromas.

title: Gastrodin alleviates acute colitis with comorbid anxiety- and depression-like behaviours rather than cognitive dysfunction by modulating gut microbiota and suppressing inflammation.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients frequently suffer from emotional disturbances, predominantly anxiety- and depression-like symptoms, and may also have cognitive dysfunction, but the mechanisms remain unclear, and no therapies targeting the gut or nervous system exist. Gastrodin (GAS), the primary active component of Gastrodia elata, has anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects. Whether GAS can alleviate acute colitis with comorbid anxiety- and depression-like behaviours or cognitive dysfunction via the gut-brain axis is unknown. Using a 3% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model, we administered GAS (240 mg/kg) by gavage for 7 days. The open field, elevated plus maze, tail suspension, and forced swimming tests showed that GAS improved behavioural abnormalities (including anxiety- and depression-like behaviours); it also restored colon length and reduced colonic histopathological injury. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that GAS reshaped the gut microbiota, increasing Sporosarcina and Nitrospirae while decreasing Clostridiaceae and Lachnospiraceae. Untargeted metabolomics indicated that GAS shifted the metabolic profile away from DSS and normalized taurine levels, and KEGG pathway analysis suggested that GAS may partially ameliorate DSS-induced metabolic disturbances by downregulating virulence-related pathways and upregulating energy metabolic pathways such as the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation relative to DSS. Western blot confirmed that GAS restored the tight junction protein Occludin and decreased TNF-α. Quantitative proteomics demonstrated that GAS reversed the aberrant expression of 191 colonic proteins. These results demonstrate correlative associations between GAS treatment and the alleviation of acute colitis and behavioural abnormalities, alongside concurrent changes in gut microbiota composition, metabolite profiles, and intestinal barrier proteins. Whether these associations reflect a causal gut-brain axis mechanism requires direct experimental validation. GAS modulates the microbiota, partially restores metabolism, repairs the gut barrier, and suppresses local inflammation, suggesting a potential gut-brain axis mechanism. These findings position GAS as a promising candidate for further mechanistic and translational investigation in IBD-associated behavioural comorbidities.

title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10-9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

title: Exercise promotes lipophagy and mitigates cognitive impairment in Alzheimer's disease through downregulating microglial TMEM9.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autophagy-lysosomal dysfunction contributes to lipid droplet (LD) accumulation, which drives pathological progression in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Exercise is reported to restore autophagy-lysosomal function and attenuate cognitive impairment in AD, but its regulation of LD deposition remains unknown. METHODS: 5×FAD transgenic mice underwent a three-month exercise intervention. Cognitive and emotional behaviors were assessed using the Morris water maze, novel object recognition, and open field test. LD deposition was evaluated by oil red O and BODIPY staining. Proteomic sequencing was performed to identify proteins affected by exercise. Pathological changes were examined by immunofluorescence, western blotting, and transmission electron microscopy. Intracerebroventricular injection of AAV was used to overexpress or knock down microglial TMEM9 to investigate the mechanisms by which physical exercise affects behavior and pathology in AD. In vitro, BV2 cells were cultured and incubated with oligomeric amyloid-β (oAβ), with or without oleic acid to induce LD formation. Chloroquine and rapamycin, which regulate autophagy-lysosomal function, were used to examine the effects of LDs on mitochondrial integrity under glucose deprivation conditions. Lentiviral or plasmid transfection was used to explore the key role of TMEM9 in regulating lipophagy, and the interaction between TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 was detected by co-immunoprecipitation. Clinically, plasma TMEM9 and ATP6AP1 levels in AD patients were measured by ELISA, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to evaluate diagnostic performance. RESULTS: Exercise mitigated cerebral LD deposition through enhanced lipophagy, preserving mitochondrial integrity and attenuating cognitive decline. Mechanistically, exercise suppressed microglial TMEM9 expression, restoring LD degradation. Tmem9 downregulation facilitated LKB1 lysosomal translocation, activating AMPK signaling. In vitro, oleic acid-induced LDs preserved mitochondrial membrane potential and increased ATP production in BV2 microglia under glucose deprivation and oAβ exposure. Tmem9 overexpression exacerbated lipophagy impairment and mitochondrial dysfunction, whereas Tmem9 knockdown enhanced lipophagy and cytoprotection. Aβ clearance was negatively regulated by TMEM9. Clinically, AD patients exhibited characteristic Aβ deposition and glucose hypometabolism, with plasma TMEM9 levels strongly correlating with p-tau217 progression. Plasma TMEM9 and the TMEM9/ATP6AP1 ratio emerged as potential AD diagnostic biomarkers (AUC=0.791 and 0.853, respectively). CONCLUSION: These findings establish exercise-induced TMEM9 inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy targeting lipidostasis to combat AD progression.

main: Intracerebroventricular injection of AAV was used to overexpress or knock down microglial TMEM9 to investigate the mechanisms by which physical exercise affects behavior and pathology in AD.

title: Compartmentalized coenzyme A and ferroptosis vulnerability in PKAN and CoPAN.
abstract: Ferroptotic vulnerability may arise from the failure of a local antioxidant defense even when whole-cell metabolite abundance appears preserved. Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) and COASY protein-associated neurodegeneration (CoPAN), two forms of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation caused by defects in coenzyme A (CoA) synthesis, provide a genetically defined setting for examining this possibility. We propose that impairment of the mitochondrial CoA pool can weaken a CoA-dependent redox defense without requiring a measurable whole-cell CoA deficit, while regional iron burden and oxidative demand lower the threshold for ferroptotic death. This model could reconcile apparently preserved bulk CoA with selective neuronal vulnerability. It is testable, remains to be validated directly in patient-derived models, and distinguishes mitochondrial CoA availability from total cellular CoA as the disease-relevant variable.
