title: Abdominal ultrasound mitigates neurodegenerative pathology and alters specific gut microbial taxa in senescence-accelerated mice.
abstract: Age-related changes in gut microbiota composition have been implicated in brain aging and cognitive decline, acting through the gut-brain axis on amyloid accumulation, tau pathology, synapse damage, and glial activation. Live microbial approaches such as probiotics, prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation address this mechanism, but they still suffer from low efficacy and unknown safety issues. We tested whether abdominal ultrasound, an approach that does not involve microbes, can alleviate age-related neurodegeneration in the senescence-accelerated mouse strain SAMP8. We treated 6-month-old male SAMP8 mice for 1 month. We then assessed behavior, neuropathology, and synaptic proteins, and quantified four pre-specified fecal bacterial taxa. Ultrasound preserved neuronal survival in the hippocampal CA3, decreased amyloid-β load in the cortex and CA3, decreased tau hyperphosphorylation in all three regions, reduced Iba-1 and GFAP immunoreactive areas, and increased synaptophysin and cortical PSD-95. Neuronal survival in the cortex and CA1 did not differ significantly from sham-treated SAMP8 mice. In the gut microbiota, ultrasound significantly reduced the enriched taxon Tyzzerella, whereas the changes in Lactobacillus, Akkermansia and Atopobiaceae were large in magnitude but not statistically significant. In an exploratory analysis, four of 64 microbiota-neuropathology associations survived correction for multiple testing. Neither object recognition memory nor spatial memory differed significantly between treated and sham-treated SAMP8 mice. Abdominal ultrasound applied to the periphery therefore reduced age-associated neuropathology in the brain, accompanied by changes in specific gut microbial taxa whose causal contribution remains untested.

title: The translational asymmetry of corpus callosotomy: Two literatures that answered different questions.
abstract: Corpus callosotomy is an established palliative operation for drug-resistant epilepsy dominated by drop attacks, and it is performed in three extents: anterior, usually of the anterior two-thirds; total, in one or two stages; and selective posterior, which preserves the genu and rostral body. Meta-analysis finds no difference between them in overall seizure reduction, a difference in drop attack control favoring the posterior approach, and a graded difference in disconnection syndrome, but there has never been a prospective head-to-head comparison, and the optimal extent of section remains undefined. A search of PubMed, Embase, and the Web of Science Core Collection identified 62 experimental studies in which the corpus callosum or another forebrain commissure was sectioned with an epilepsy-related outcome, spanning 1948-2026 across six species and every major seizure model. This literature is neither absent nor recent. What it has almost never done is vary the extent of section: the few studies that varied it took the laterality of kindling transfer or of interictal synchrony as the endpoint, never seizure control and never cognitive cost. No study compares the three extents against a common outcome; none models the selective posterior operation as it is defined clinically; none randomizes between extents; and none combines graded disconnection with time-locked bilateral electrophysiology, diffusion-based verification of the fibers divided, and a behavioral read-out in the same animals. The effect of section is also bidirectional: focal seizures may intensify through loss of transcallosal inhibition, and in the pentylenetetrazol model callosal section paradoxically facilitates convulsions, which limits chemoconvulsant preparations. The asymmetry between the clinical and experimental literatures is therefore one of method rather than of volume or attention: the two answered different questions, and the question the clinical field now asks requires a manipulation the experimental literature has never performed. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Surgeons can treat severe epilepsies by cutting the bundle of fibers that joins the two halves of the brain, but they do not agree on how much of it to cut. We searched three databases and found 62 animal studies of this operation going back to 1948. Almost none of them compared different amounts of cutting, and none looked at the newest version of the operation. Answering the surgeons' question will require a new kind of animal experiment rather than more reading of the old ones.

title: PBRM1 Deficiency in Microglia Leads to Excessive Neurogenesis and Autism-Like Behaviors via the CCL5-CCR1/5-β-catenin Signaling Axis.
abstract: The prevalence of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder with limited effective therapeutic drugs, has been rising worldwide. Missense mutations in Polybromo 1 (Pbrm1), a core component of the SWI/SNF (switch/sucrose non-fermentable) chromatin remodeling complex, have been identified as a risk factor for ASD; however, whether PBRM1 loss of function contributes to the pathogenesis remains elusive. Here we provide direct evidence that microglial PBRM1 deficiency leads to altered microglial clusters, excessive neurogenesis, and ASD-like behaviors in mice. Integrated molecular analyses reveal that PBRM1 directly binds to the Ccl5 promoter and represses the expression of CCL5. Elevated CCL5 promotes the proliferation and neuronal differentiation of neural stem/progenitor cells (NSPCs) via the CCR1/5-β-catenin signaling pathway. Importantly, pharmacological blockade of CCR1/5 ameliorates behavioral deficits in Pbrm1 cKO mice. Together, these findings identify a previously unrecognized microglia-NSPC communication mechanism linking PBRM1 dysfunction to aberrant neurodevelopment and suggest the CCL5-CCR1/5 axis as a potential therapeutic target for ASD.

title: Feature selection and dimensionality reduction in multi-omics.
abstract: High-throughput multi-omics technologies generate high-dimensional, heterogeneous and noisy datasets, making robust biomarker discovery and disease modelling challenging. This review critically examines dimensionality reduction and representation strategies for multi-omics analysis while distinguishing three related but different goals: feature selection, feature extraction/representation learning, and multi-omics integration. We use sparse canonical correlation analysis (sCCA), variational autoencoders (VAEs), and graph convolutional networks (GCNs) as representative case studies spanning sparse linear, probabilistic deep-learning, and graph-based approaches. Rather than treating these methods as interchangeable, we compare their data requirements, assumptions, interpretability, ability to accommodate non-linearity and missing modalities, computational demands, and validation needs. Applications across cancer, cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disease, and across bulk, single-cell, spatial and imaging multi-omics are summarized in comparative tables. We conclude with practical guidance for matching method families to biological questions and emphasize that robust biomarker claims require leakage-free model development, stability assessment and independent validation.

title: Molecular Signatures of HIV-Induced Neuroinflammation and Neurodegeneration in Human Cerebral Organoids: Identification of Therapeutic Targets for NeuroHIV.
abstract: HIV-associated neurological complications remain a major concern in people living with HIV (PWH), even under effective viral suppression with combination antiretroviral therapy (cART), underscoring unresolved mechanisms driving HIV-related neurodegeneration. To address this gap, we used HIV-1-infected human cerebral organoids (hCOs) containing microglia as a physiologically relevant three-dimensional model of the central nervous system (CNS) and validated key findings in the brain region of simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV)-infected, cART-treated rhesus macaque model. Integrated single-nucleus RNA sequencing with ATAC-seq (multi-omics), identifies cell-type-specific alterations in dual innate immune-driven inflammatory signaling pathways across neural and glial populations in hCOs. Microglia were preferentially infected and activated, initiating IL-17A-mediated cascades involving IFN-γ/STAT1, CEBPB, and NF-κB signaling. These pathways converged with cGAS-STING and Notch-NEURL1 signaling, both associated with neuroinflammation and synaptic dysfunction. cART suppressed viral replication, reduced IL-17A-mediated neuroinflammation, improved mitochondrial function, and restored synaptic gene expression. Collectively, these findings identify dysregulation of IL-17A, STAT1, CEBPB, and cGAS-STING signaling as key molecular drivers of HIV-associated neuroinflammation. They also establish a potential mechanistic link between IL-17A signaling and microglial remodeling, providing a translational framework for the development of CNS-targeted therapies in PWH.

title: TBK1-mediated phosphorylation of WIPI2 links bacteria recognition to autophagosome formation in xenophagy.
abstract: Xenophagy, a selective autophagy pathway, is a critical innate immune defense mechanism that targets pathogens for lysosomal degradation. However, the molecular mechanisms enabling autophagosomes to specifically recognize and engulf bacteria remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify WIPI2, a core component that drives autophagosome biogenesis, as a novel phosphorylation substrate of TBK1 during Salmonella Typhimurium infection. We demonstrate that TBK1 phosphorylates WIPI2 at Ser96, which enhances its interaction with ATG16L1 and its binding to PtdIns3P. Crucially, the recruitment of WIPI2 to intracellular bacteria is dependent on its interaction with ATG16L1, which is localized to the Salmonella-containing vacuole. Furthermore, TBK1-mediated phosphorylation of WIPI2 is required for efficient bacterial clearance. Collectively, our findings reveal a molecular mechanism whereby TBK1-mediated phosphorylation of WIPI2 directs localized phagophore expansion around invading bacteria, thereby bridging bacterial recognition with autophagosome assembly.Abbreviations: ATG: autophagy related; ATG5: autophagy related 5; ATG16L1: autophagy related 16 like 1; CALCOCO2/NDP52: calcium binding and coiled-coil domain 2; CFU: colony-forming units; GFP: green fluorescent protein; GST: glutathione S-transferase; IL6: interleukin 6; KO: knockout; LPS: lipopolysaccharides; MAP1LC3/LC3: microtubule associated protein 1 light chain 3; OPTN: optineurin; PtdIns: phosphatidylinositol; PtdIns3P: phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate; RB1CC1/FIP200: RB1 inducible coiled-coil 1; RFP: red fluorescent protein;S. title: Mincle exacerbates neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neurodegeneration via synergistic crosstalk with TLR4.
abstract: Microglial activation and subsequent neuroinflammation are critically implicated in the pathogenesis and progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Macrophage-inducible C-type lectin (Mincle) is a pivotal pattern recognition receptor that participates in the regulation of innate immune responses. Nevertheless, the functional role of Mincle in mediating dopaminergic neuronal injury in PD remains poorly defined. In the present study, we observed a marked upregulation of Mincle expression in microglia in PD mouse models. Pharmacological inhibition of Mincle via Anti-Mincle antibody treatment effectively alleviated LPS-triggered dopaminergic neuronal loss in the SN and rescued motor behavioral impairments in mice. Additionally, Mincle blockade promoted microglial phenotypic transformation, driving a shift from the pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype. Mechanistically, pharmacological blockade of either TLR4 or NF-κB signaling abrogated LPS-induced Mincle upregulation. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays further confirmed that the NF-κB/P65 subunit directly binds to the promoter region of the Mincle, verifying that the TLR4/NF-κB signaling serves as a critical upstream regulatory pathway for Mincle expression. Notably, this study provides the first in vivo evidence that Mincle activation by a Mincle-specific agonist trehalose-6,6-dibehenate (TDB) induces robust dopaminergic neurotoxicity and motor dysfunction in C57BL/6 J mice, accompanied by significant elevations in the expression of the pro-inflammatory and microglial activation markers iNOS and CD68. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that synergistic crosstalk between the Mincle-Syk signaling cascade and the TLR4/NF-κB pathway sustains the pro-inflammatory M1 microglial phenotype, thereby triggering progressive dopaminergic neuronal damage in the SN. This study uncovers a previously unrecognized pathogenic role of Mincle in neuroinflammation-mediated neurodegeneration, highlighting Mincle as a promising novel therapeutic target for PD intervention.

title: Animal models for investigating post-stroke cognitive impairment: A neurovascular trafficking perspective.
abstract: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is a major cause of long-term disability after ischemic stroke, yet its mechanisms remain incompletely explained by infarct volume, lesion location, or conventional vascular risk factors alone. Animal models are indispensable for clarifying how ischemic injury evolves into delayed cognitive dysfunction and for determining which mechanisms are experimentally tractable, reproducible, and translationally relevant. This review examines PSCI from a neurovascular trafficking perspective, focusing on how laboratory animal models can be used to investigate secretory pathway stress, endolysosomal dysfunction, autophagy-lysosomal flux, extracellular vesicle signaling, blood-brain barrier disruption, glial reactivity, myelin debris clearance, white matter injury, and cognition-relevant behavioral phenotypes. Rodent models of transient or permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion, photothrombotic stroke, embolic stroke, chronic cerebral hypoperfusion, bilateral carotid artery stenosis, and subcortical white-matter injury each reproduce selected components of the human PSCI spectrum. No single model fully captures the temporal, vascular, cellular, and cognitive complexity of human PSCI; therefore, model selection should be driven by the mechanistic question, disease phase, vascular pathology, cellular compartment, cognitive domain, and welfare burden under investigation. The central argument is not that neurovascular trafficking failure is already a proven causal pathway, but that well-designed animal studies can test, refine, or falsify this hypothesis. Future studies should integrate model validity, translational rigor, and welfare refinement through longitudinal cognitive testing, multimodal imaging, cell-specific molecular profiling, extracellular vesicle phenotyping, intervention-based validation, randomization, blinding, sample-size justification, humane endpoints, perioperative care, and transparent reporting.

title: A microglial basis for fragile X syndrome via impairment of FMRP-regulated lysosomal function.
abstract: Silencing of the FMRP-encoding FMR1 gene results in fragile X syndrome (FXS), the most common inheritable intellectual disability and autism. FMRP regulates various neuronal functions but clinical trials targeting neurons have failed, suggesting unrecognized disease mechanisms. We find that mice with selective Fmr1 deletion in microglia exhibit audiogenic seizures (AGS) and parvalbumin (PV) neuron loss, recapitulating two key phenotypes observed in FXS (Fmr1-/y) mice. By combining snRNA-Seq and RNA immunoprecipitation, we identify several lysosomal mRNAs as FMRP binding targets. FMRP promotes lysosomal protein expression and its deficiency disrupts lysosomal function in microglia. Notably, FMRP depletion reduces Grn-encoded secretory progranulin and increases PV neuron apoptosis in immature brains. PV neuron density is decreased similarly in Grn+/-, Fmr1-/y, and Grn+/-;Fmr1-/y mice, and progranulin overexpression rescues AGS and PV neuron loss in Fmr1-/y mice. Thus, our study identifies microglia and progranulin as critical regulators of FXS pathogenesis and potential targets for FXS therapy.

title: Molecular recognition of axonal injury-associated candidate hub genes and predicted inhibitors across Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract: UNLABELLED: Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) have converging molecular pathologies such as neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and axonal degeneration, but do not have broadly effective disease-modifying therapies. A novel computational strategy was used in this study with an integrated in-silico pipeline to determine common candidate hub genes across AD, PD, and ALS and to computationally screen candidate inhibitors. The gene expression datasets were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus database and analyzed with limma R package for blood-derived gene expression datasets for AD (GSE63060), PD (GSE99039) and ALS (GSE112680). A multi-dataset intersection analysis revealed 138 genes commonly upregulated and 0 commonly downregulated genes, which were functionally enriched in immune regulation, apoptotic signaling and mitochondrial instability pathways. Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified three key genes (MMP9, PTPN6 and TNFRSF1A) as high-confidence candidate hub genes for AD, PD, and ALS. The ZINC library of 34,853 compounds was screened for drug-like properties using QikProp to yield 16,466 drug-like compounds. Based on the comparative screening results, the structure of MMP9 (PDB ID: 8K5Y) was chosen for further analysis and two of the selected compounds ZINC04582833, ZINC00047690 were identified as the two highest ranked compounds with docking scores of - 10.4 and - 9.7 kcal/mol respectively. Both complexes were further evaluated by 100 ns MD simulations, showing RMSD profile stability, maintained secondary structure for both complexes. The results in this study make ZINC04582833 and ZINC00047690 computationally prioritized candidates for shared neurodegenerative targets for experimental validation. title: Cryo-EM advances in TDP-43 amyloid fibrils structure determination.
abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a DNA/RNA-binding protein whose pathological aggregation characterizes a spectrum of neurodegenerative disorders known as TDP-43 proteinopathies, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Recent breakthroughs in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have revolutionized our understanding of these diseases by resolving the atomic structures of TDP-43 amyloid fibrils. These structural insights have been pivotal in elucidating the transition from functional liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to irreversible solid-state aggregation. This review synthesizes key cryo-EM findings from 2019 to 2026, encompassing fibrils formed by the full-length low-complexity domain, disease-relevant core fragments, and filaments extracted directly from patient tissues, as well as the pathological implications of distinct structural polymorphs. These findings not only deepen our understanding of the brain science aspects of the pathogenesis of TDP-43 proteinopathies, but also provide an important structural basis for the development of specific conformational diagnostic methods and targeted therapeutic drugs.

title: Biallelic PAX6 Variants in an Adult With Severe Microphthalmia and Preserved Intellectual Function.
abstract: PAX6 encodes a dosage-sensitive transcription factor that is essential for eye development. Heterozygous PAX6 disease is well characterized, but biallelic disease is extremely rare and has been associated with anophthalmia, severe brain malformations, and perinatal lethality. Here we report the first adult patient with biallelic pathogenic PAX6 variants and describe a novel phenotype that includes severe microphthalmia, anosmia, and autism spectrum disorder, Level 1. Notably, intellectual function was preserved. Genome sequencing revealed compound heterozygosity for the missense variant c.622C>T p.(Arg208Trp), inherited from the patient's mother diagnosed with sclerocornea and iris hypoplasia, and the nonsense variant c.718C>T p.(Arg240*), inherited from the patient's father diagnosed with aniridia. We compare the phenotype and genotype with previously reported biallelic patients and observe that the neurological phenotype of the patient fits the pattern observed in PAX6 haploinsufficiency. We propose that the severe microphthalmia is the result of haploinsufficiency and a hypomorphic, eye-restricted effect of the missense variant, which is predicted to affect the DNA-binding homeodomain of PAX6. Together, these findings expand the phenotypic spectrum of biallelic PAX6 disease and suggest that the homeodomain may have a tissue-specific role that is critical for eye development but largely dispensable for brain development.

title: TGF-β Inhibition Attenuates Tau Accumulation and Neurodegeneration in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Patient-Derived Organoids.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a devastating 4-repeat tauopathy with no approved disease-modifying treatments. Recent evidence showed increased transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) levels in PSP patient-derived ventral midbrain organoids (vMOs) and serum neuronally derived exosomes. OBJECTIVE: This study investigated whether TGF-β pharmacological inhibition could mitigate PSP pathology in vMOs. METHODS: Ninety-six vMOs were generated from induced pluripotent stem cells from two PSP-Richardson's syndrome patients and two healthy control donors (HCs). From day 60 to day 90, PSP organoids were (1) exposed to TGF-β receptor I inhibitor (SB431542); (2) exposed to recombinant TGF-β1, TGF-β2, and TGF-β3; or (3) untreated. At day 90, several tau species were assessed by immunoblotting; neurodegeneration was evaluated through TUNEL assay and immunofluorescence (tyrosine hydroxylase [TH], neurofilament light chain [NfL]); astrocytic activation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) marker was evaluated by immunofluorescence, and histopathological hallmarks were evaluated by immunohistochemistry. An HC-derived organoid subgroup was exposed to the treatment conditions to assess potential toxicity. RESULTS: At day 90, untreated PSP-derived vMOs exhibited increased phosphorylated tau levels (Ser396, Thr181, Ser202/Ser205 [AT8]) compared with HC-derived vMOs, dopaminergic neuron loss (reduced TH, increased NfL), and astrocytic reactivity (increased GFAP), along with PSP characteristic tau deposition. Tau hyperphosphorylation, neurodegeneration, and astrocytic reactivity were all markedly reduced in PSP-derived vMOs treated with TGF-β receptor I inhibitor. Conversely, exposure to TGF-β exacerbated these features. No toxic effects were observed in HC vMOs exposed to treatment conditions. CONCLUSIONS: Pharmacological inhibition of TGF-β signaling prevented key PSP molecular alterations in patient-derived organoids. These findings support further research and pave the way for future investigation of TGF-β-targeting strategies in clinical trials in patients with PSP. © 2026 The Author(s). title: iPSC neurodegenerative disease initiative isogenic CAG repeat iPSC line for Huntington's disease.
abstract: Purpose of ResearchThe generation of iPSC lines expressing 21, 56 and 79 glutamine repeats within the HTT protein and homozygous KO of HTT in the KOLF2.1J background as an additional disease series within the iPSC Neurodegenerative Disease Initiative (iNDI) collection.Major FindingsAll iPSCs, even those expressing long repeats of 79Q or HTT KO, were capable of differentiating to striatal and cortical neurons, astrocytes and microglia using established protocols. General quality control stains and morphological analyses are described for each differentiation. A selected set of assays were carried out on differentiated cells; expanded repeat expressing astrocytes showed altered expression of astrocyte protein markers and morphological characteristics, and striatal neurons showed altered DARPP-32/CTIP2 colocalization. mRNAseq carried out for striatal neurons showed high similarities in gene expression changes between 79Q and KO lines compared to the unexpanded repeat.ConclusionsThe KOLF2.1J isogenic CAG repeat series serves as a community resource to study HD mechanisms with the potential for direct comparison across other neurodegenerative diseases through the iNDI collection.

title: Six3 promoting the migration and neural differentiation of BMSCs via Btg2‑mediated Akt signaling pathway activation: A therapeutic strategy for stroke.
abstract: Bone marrow‑derived mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) transplantation holds therapeutic potential for stroke; however, but its effectiveness requires optimization. The transcription factor Sine Oculis Homeobox Homolog 3 (Six3) regulates processes crucial for BMSC therapy, such as neural cell proliferation and differentiation. However, whether Six3‑modified BMSCs exert enhanced therapeutic effects on stroke remains unknown. In the present study, mouse BMSCs were isolated and identified using surface markers. Six3‑overexpressing BMSCs exhibited enhanced proliferative, migratory and neural differentiation capacities. RNA‑sequencing analysis comparing the gene expression profiles of BMSCs with and without Six3 overexpression identified BTG Anti‑Proliferation Factor 2 (Btg2) as an upregulated gene (log2FC=1.45, P<0.05) in Six3‑overexpressing cells. Further investigations revealed that Six3 directly binds to the TGATACTGTCT sequence within the Btg2 promoter and activates its transcription. Btg2 knockdown abolished the effects of Six3 overexpression. Mechanistically, Six3 promoted Akt phosphorylation via Btg2, enhancing BMSC viability and neural differentiation. A mouse model of stroke was established using transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO, 1.5‑h occlusion and 24‑h reperfusion). BMSCs were administered via tail vein injection at the onset of reperfusion. GFP expression detected in brain tissue at 24 h post‑reperfusion confirmed successful the homing of BMSCs to the brain. The transplantation of Six3‑overexpressing BMSCs ameliorated brain pathology, reducing apoptosis and cerebral infarct volume. Notably, Six3‑modified BMSCs demonstrated a significantly greater therapeutic efficacy than unmodified BMSCs. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that Six3 enhances the therapeutic properties of BMSCs by transcriptionally activating Btg2, which promotes Akt phosphorylation. These findings provide novel mechanistic insight into the optimization of stem cell therapy in stroke.

title: Extended field-of-view two-photon imaging in the deep brain of freely behaving mice using lightweight microfabricated corrective optics.
abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

title: Septins as novel regulators of podosome cluster organization and dynamics in human immature dendritic cells.
abstract: Podosomes are actin-rich adhesions that enable cells to probe their environment, migrate across tissue boundaries, and degrade extracellular matrix. They are often organized in clusters, where their spatial organization is governed by complex actin networks, including a vinculin-associated ventral network and a myosin IIA-associated dorsal network. The molecular composition and mechanisms coordinating these networks, however, remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify septins as novel constituents of the podosome network in human immature dendritic cells. Using super-resolution microscopy, we show that septin 2, 7 and 9 are excluded from the actin core and do not colocalize with the canonical podosome ring. Instead, septins localize to the dorsal actin network that interconnects individual podosomes. Disruption of the septin network does not prevent podosome formation but alters the spatiotemporal organization of the podosome actin network. Furthermore, although septins and myosin IIA do not directly colocalize, septin perturbation leads to axial mislocalization and reduced activity of myosin IIA. Together, our findings identify septins as novel regulators of podosome cluster organization, adding an additional layer of complexity to the cytoskeletal coordination of these structures.

title: Bridging language phenotypes, neural dynamics and gene regulation in autism.
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs) affect approximately 1% of the global population, with prevalence rising over recent decades. Although ASDs are heritable (~70%), translating genetic findings into effective therapeutics remains challenging due to the vast number of implicated risk genes (>700) and the limited influence of individual genes on disease expression. Their collective impact and convergent expression patterns of small-effect genes provide insights into ASD-related neurobiological mechanisms. Current interventions remain symptom-focused and do not address underlying neurodevelopmental mechanisms. Emerging approaches in functional genomics offer new insights into ASD pathogenesis by exploring gene expression diversity, yet clinical applications remain distant. Language deficits are among the most frequent and disabling features of ASD, profoundly affecting individuals' and families' quality of life. Recent evidence from neuroimaging and electrophysiology studies suggests disrupted neural oscillatory dynamics are linked to language deficits in ASD. Several ASD-associated genes have been implicated in biological pathways involved in the regulation of brain oscillatory dynamics, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between genetic variation, altered brain rhythms, and language impairment. We propose a neurophysiological imaging genetics framework that leverages neural oscillatory profiles as endophenotypes for targeted investigation and as functional readouts of gene expression. Within this framework, neuromodulation is proposed as an experimental approach to investigate and potentially modulate altered oscillatory dynamics associated with speech communication deficits in ASD, while integrating oscillation-related ASD candidate genes into a symptom-oriented model of functional genomics. This approach shows how integrating genetic variation, non-invasive neuroimaging, and behavioral phenotypes can advance our understanding of ASD and inform targeted, mechanism-based interventions.

title: Modeling Moyamoya disease using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells and organoids.
abstract: The underlying mechanisms of Moyamoya disease (MMD), a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder marked by distal internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion and the formation of fragile collaterals, remain poorly understood, in part because conventional models fail to capture the genetic, vascular, and neurovascular complexity of human MMD. Driven by recent advances in disease modeling, MMD research has moved beyond early endothelial progenitor cell studies toward patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based platforms. Here, we summarize the generation and validation of MMD-specific iPSCs and their differentiation into endothelial cells (ECs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and related vascular lineages, and we discuss how two-dimensional (2D) iPSC-based models have provided insights into impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal VSMC behavior, and disrupted vascular cell interactions. We then highlight the emerging use of three-dimensional vascular and neurovascular organoids, which reproduce cellular heterogeneity, vessel-like organization, and neurovascular unit interactions more closely than conventional 2D cultures. These models may provide a more integrated platform for investigating the complex vascular pathophysiology of MMD. Finally, we discuss future directions for MMD modeling, including the integration of multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-mediated genome editing with patient-derived iPSC and organoid platforms. These approaches may help clarify genotype-phenotype relationships, RNF213-dependent and RNF213-independent mechanisms, and disease-relevant molecular pathways. With further standardization and validation, iPSC- and organoid-based models could support mechanistic studies, therapeutic screening, and personalized disease modeling. Our review underscores the emerging role of patient-derived stem cell and organoid technologies in advancing MMD research and in informing future translational efforts.

title: Unraveling the Genotype-Phenotype Landscape of Kleefstra Syndrome Through EHMT1 Variant Analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Kleefstra syndrome type 1 (KLEFS1) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in EHMT1, which play a key role in epigenetic regulation. Core features include global developmental delay (GDD), intellectual disability (ID), facial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects (CHDs), and neuropsychiatric manifestations. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with KLEFS1 evaluated at Seoul National University Hospital between January 2022 and April 2025. Genetic diagnoses were made using chromosomal microarray or whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, and clinical data were extracted from medical records. To enhance statistical power, we conducted a joint analysis with established cohorts of at least 30 clinically characterized patients. RESULTS: Among the 15 patients with KLEFS1, 14 (93.3%) exhibited GDD or ID, with frequent comorbidities such as CHDs (8/12, 66.7%), orthopaedic manifestations (6/12, 50.0%), epilepsy (6/15, 40.0%), and sleep problems (4/11, 36.4%). Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in 10 of the 12 patients (83.3%), including pituitary anomalies in 2 (16.7%). By combining our data with recently published multicenter international cohorts, we assessed genotype-phenotype correlations by comparing the clinical features of 202 patients with different variant subtypes. Patients with multigene deletions had a significantly higher prevalence of CHDs (53.5% vs 25.8%, p value = 2 × 10-4), cortical visual impairment (12.5% vs 1.7%, p value = 0.004), microcephaly (37.1% vs 17.8%, p value = 0.009), corpus callosum abnormalities (17.9% vs 5.9%, p value = 0.02), and hearing impairment (39.7% vs 25.6%, p value = 0.04) than those with single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) or short insertions/deletions (indels), in addition to the previously identified features including epilepsy, constipation, and short stature. We also observed that a recurrent EHMT1 variant (p.Arg948Trp), identified in multiple unrelated patients, was linked to significant phenotypic heterogeneity, including late-onset neurocognitive regression. DISCUSSION: Our study showed that patients with multigene deletions are significantly more likely to exhibit multiorgan involvement, including CHDs, cortical visual impairments, microcephaly, corpus callosum abnormalities, and hearing impairments, compared with those with SNVs or indels, emphasizing the importance of genotype-informed management. We report pituitary gland abnormalities in KLEFS1, expanding the phenotypic and neuroimaging spectrum of KLEFS1. The patient showing regression in their 30s necessitates long-term, comprehensive studies to support care.

title: Spatiotemporal AI-based modeling of gene regulation and variant effects in the developing human brain using Seal.
abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation in the developing human brain remains a central challenge in neuroscience, particularly in transient cell types and developmental stages where data are limited. We present Seal, an interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) transfer learning framework for genome-based modeling of gene expression and variant effects with spatiotemporal resolution across 26 regions, 30 cell types and 7 developmental stages. Seal predictions provide mechanistic interpretation by linking variants to transcriptional regulators in a spatiotemporal context. Applying Seal to genome-wide association studies, we identify shared and distinct regulatory architectures across six neuropsychiatric conditions that align with clinical trajectories. In the Simons Simplex Collection autism cohort whole-genome data, Seal uncovers a significant burden of de novo regulatory variants in transient fetal excitatory neurons, revealing cell-type-specific and stage-specific effects. By connecting genetic variation to spatiotemporal regulatory programs, Seal offers a general framework for uncovering mechanisms of human brain development and disease.

title: A PTPRO inhibitor Pi mitigates endotoxemia-induced encephalopathy-mediated blood-brain barrier disruption through cytoskeletal regulation.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Septic encephalopathy (SE) is closely associated with disruption of blood-brain barrier (BBB), resulting in neurological deficits and poor clinical outcomes. Protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) regulates disease states by dephosphorylating membrane-associated proteins and modulating intracellular signalling. Here we have examined the role of PTPRO in regulating BBB permeability and have assessed a PTPRO inhibitor (Pi) in mitigating BBB disruption during endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Genetic and pharmacological approaches, including PTPRO overexpression, knockdown or deficiency and Pi treatment, were used to evaluate endothelial dysfunction in bEND.3 cells, primary mouse brain microvascular endothelial cells and an LPS-induced murine model of endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. Barrier dysfunction, cytoskeletal remodelling and signalling events were assessed using permeability assays, immunoblotting, immunofluorescence and in vivo BBB leakage analyses. KEY RESULTS: LPS increased PTPRO expression in brain tissue from endotoxemic mice and cerebral endothelial cells. Elevated PTPRO promoted F-actin reorganization, stress fibre formation and intercellular gap formation, whereas Pi treatment or PTPRO silencing attenuated these changes. PTPRO overexpression worsened endothelial barrier dysfunction, while Pi reduced thrombin-induced permeability in bEND.3 cells and wild-type primary endothelial cells. Primary endothelial cells from PTPRO-deficient mice were protected. Mechanistically, PTPRO regulated cytoskeletal dynamics through the ErbB2-Rho-MLC2 pathway. In vivo, Pi treatment and PTPRO deficiency reduced BBB leakage, with limited effects on inflammatory cytokines. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: These findings identify PTPRO as an important regulator of BBB disruption in endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy and support pharmacological targeting of PTPRO as a potential strategy for preserving sepsis-associated BBB injury.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen reveals that Wnt signaling regulates lipid accumulation in APOE4 oligodendrocytes.
abstract: APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, yet the cellular mechanisms linking APOE variants to disease risk remain unclear. We previously found that APOE4 expression causes lipid droplet accumulation in oligodendrocytes, reducing myelination, but the underlying mechanisms were unknown. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen and assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) sequencing in human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived oligodendrocytes, we identified decreased Wnt signaling and overactive glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B) as key regulators of lipid-droplet accumulation. Genetic and pharmacological inhibition of GSK3B reduced lipid droplets in APOE4 oligodendrocytes and increased myelination in three-dimensional iPSC-derived brain organoids. Pharmacological GSK3B inhibition also reduced lipid droplets and improved myelination in APOE4;PS19 tau transgenic mice. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework linking Wnt/GSK3B signaling to APOE4-driven disruptions in oligodendrocyte lipid metabolism and myelination, pointing to GSK3B as a potential therapeutic target for APOE4-associated Alzheimer's disease.

title: Female iPSC X chromosome inactivation erosion and its transcriptomic effects during CRISPR gene editing and neural differentiation.
abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with CRISPR editing, are commonly used for studying neurodevelopmental disorders. Female iPSCs gradually lose the expression of the noncoding X chromosome inactive-specific transcript (XIST), leading to random X chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion that affects both X-linked and autosomal gene expression. However, the effects of CRISPR editing and neural differentiation on XCI erosion and how this may confound a real-world analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are poorly understood. Here, we analyzed hundreds of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) samples of CRISPR-edited iPSC lines for 66 genes and the matched single-neuron RNA-seq data. We found variable XCI in CRISPR-edited female iPSCs, which was largely preserved in iPSC-derived neurons and predominantly influenced X-linked genes. Mechanistically, XIST mediates allele-specific epigenetic regulation of both X-linked and autosomal genes, with the former showing stronger allele-specific expression (ASE) bias that affects neurodevelopmental genes. These results have significant implications in hiPSC-based modeling of neurodevelopmental disorders.

overview: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with CRISPR editing, are commonly used for studying neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: FOXG1 spatiotemporally orchestrates subtype fate specification and patch/matrix identity of striatal spiny projection neurons.
abstract: The striatum consists of three main spiny projection neuron subtypes, direct-pathway neurons (dSPNs), indirect-pathway neurons (iSPNs), and recently identified eccentric striatal neurons (eSPNs) with these SPNs organized into two complementary compartments, the patch and the matrix. However, the cellular basis underlying subtype specification especially that of eSPNs, and mechanisms governing the complementary patterning remain unclear. Here, employing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) combined with loss-of-function we reveal that eSPNs share more developmental similarities with iSPNs and the transcription factor Foxg1 promotes dSPN and iSPN fates but suppresses eSPN fate in ventral region of the lateral ganglionic eminence lineage. Deletion of Foxg1 in progenitors forces both dSPNs and iSPNs into an eSPN fate. While postmitotic Foxg1 deletion impairs patch/matrix identity and leads to SPN aggregation. We identify FOXG1-driven transcriptional programs and key transcription factors that specify each striatal SPN subtype and patch/matrix identity, and uncover FOXG1 directly regulated cell migration- and cell adhesion-related molecules that control SPN migration. Our findings provide insights into striatal development.

title: An integrative transcriptomic atlas of ALS and aging skeletal muscle defines shared and distinct molecular programs of degeneration.
abstract: Skeletal muscle atrophy and weakness resulting from loss of motor neuron innervation are shared hallmarks of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and age-associated sarcopenia. However, muscle wasting in ALS is rapid and severe, whereas sarcopenia progresses gradually over decades, peaking at an advanced age. The molecular mechanisms underlying muscle wasting in these conditions remain incompletely defined. Here, we used the SOD1G93A ALS mouse model and wild-type mice across the lifespan to generate an integrated single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of skeletal muscle, mapping changes associated with ALS and aging. This atlas is complemented by structural and functional analyses. Our results identify transcriptionally distinct condition-specific myonuclear states, including disease-responsive programs within synaptic myonuclei at the neuromuscular junction, that are shared or distinct between the two conditions. Notably, at early stages, muscle from ALS mice exhibits molecular hallmarks of aged muscle at the myofiber level, indicating premature aging and reinforcing aging as a risk factor in ALS. At advanced disease stages and in old age, myonuclear subpopulations follow similar degenerative pathways in fast glycolytic fibers, consistent with their loss in both conditions. However, a distinct ALS-enriched myonuclei subpopulation displays uniquely regulated genes not observed in aged muscle, potentially underlying the more rapid and severe pathology observed in ALS. This atlas maps shared and divergent mechanisms of muscle degeneration in ALS and sarcopenia and provides a resource for identifying therapeutic targets tailored to each condition.

title: Mitochondrial apoptosis imaged by high-throughput confocal microscopy.
abstract: Mitochondrial programmed cell death (i.e. intrinsic apoptosis) is regulated through the formation of pro-apoptotic protein complexes at the mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM), which permeabilize the MOM and commit the cell to die. This step is modulated by mitochondrial dynamics. To capture this, we treated cells with the mitochondrial dynamics inhibitor M1 before inducing apoptosis with actinomycin D (ActD), and imaged them by high-throughput spinning-disk confocal microscopy. In mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) we followed apoptosis by long-term live-cell imaging, and in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) we stained fixed cells for the pro-apoptotc protein BAX at mitochondria. Here, we provide a description of these two large-scale microscopy datasets. Dataset 1 contains 637,632 images of MEFs imaged as time series after labelling of mitochondrial morphology and integrity with the mitochondrial membrane potential-sensitive dye tetramethylrhodamine-ethylester (TMRE) and apoptosis with Annexin V-FITC. The dataset also contains a digital phase contrast channel which can be useful to track cells. Dataset 2 contains 9,504 images of hiPSCs with immunofluorescence labelling of BAX and COX IV. The datasets are made available through the BioImage Archive repository.

title: Modeling human neurodegeneration with iPSCs: opportunities, limitations, and the challenge of aging.
abstract: Most neurodegenerative diseases reflect patient-specific combinations of polygenic risk variants interacting with aging and environmental factors, rather than a single causative mutation. Phase III clinical trial failure rates for neurodegenerative indications exceed 95%, reflecting in part the limitations of existing preclinical systems to fully model the human genetic context of disease. Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have the potential to address this shortcoming by faithfully recapitulating human cell biology and preserving each patient's complete genetic architecture. This Review examines iPSC-based models of neurodegeneration across three themes. First, we discuss mechanisms revealed by these models, from convergent pathways uncovered by familial mutations to early evidence that sporadic disease biology is accessible at sufficient cohort scale. Second, we evaluate culture systems from 2-dimensional monocultures to organoids, examining how increasing complexity expands addressable biological questions while introducing trade-offs. Third, we address the aging problem: reprogramming erases epigenetic signatures of donor aging, removing the cellular context in which late-onset sporadic neurodegeneration emerges. We discuss strategies approximating aging in iPSC-derived neurons and highlight direct conversion strategies that preserve native epigenetic age, enabling access to age-dependent phenotypes. We propose a framework matching model systems to biological questions, improving mechanistic understanding and therapeutic development.

title: MD2-IN-1 restores microglial lysosomal function and attenuates amyloid pathology through TREM2-associated signaling in 5×FAD mice.
abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a central regulator of microglial adaptation during Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the development of small-molecule modulators associated with TREM2 signaling remains limited. Here, through a consensus pharmacophore-guided virtual screening strategy, MD2-IN-1 was identified as a candidate small molecule associated with TREM2 signaling. Biolayer interferometry and cellular thermal shift assays supported cellular target engagement related to TREM2 (KD = 13.85 μM). In Aβ-stimulated BV2 microglia, MD2-IN-1 increased SYK phosphorylation, promoted Aβ uptake, and shifted microglial responses toward a less proinflammatory phenotype. These effects were markedly attenuated following Trem2 knockdown, indicating the involvement of the TREM2-SYK signaling pathway. Mechanistically, MD2-IN-1 restored lysosomal acidification and increased the expression of the V-ATPase subunits ATP6v0c and ATP6v0a1, accompanied by increased intracellular Aβ degradation. In 5×FAD mice, chronic MD2-IN-1 administration improved cognitive performance without detectable behavioral abnormalities compared with WT animals. Multimodal PET imaging demonstrated reduced amyloid deposition and attenuated neuroinflammatory signals, which were further supported by histological analyses showing decreased plaque burden, reduced inflammatory microglial responses, and preserved neuronal integrity. In addition, MD2-IN-1 reduced P62 accumulation and restored ATP6v0c expression in vivo, whereas these effects were partially attenuated by pharmacological inhibition of TREM2. Collectively, these findings identify MD2-IN-1 as a small-molecule modulator associated with TREM2 signaling that restores microglial lysosomal degradative function and promotes Aβ clearance in AD models, providing pharmacological support for targeting adaptive microglial responses in AD.

title: Beyond PROTACs: Conditional Technologies and New Frontiers.
abstract: This chapter surveys the post-PROTAC landscape of targeted protein degradation (TPD), covering conditional activation, new degradation modalities, and proximity-driven editing of post-translational modifications (PTMs). Condition-activated PROTACs harness prodrugs responsive to irradiation or the tumor microenvironment and nanoparticle-based platforms to achieve spatiotemporally resolved protein degradation. The targetable space is further expanded by molecular glues that recruit neosubstrates to E3 ligases, endocytosis-lysosome targeting chimeras that clear extracellular and membrane proteins, and autophagy-lysosome strategies that degrade aggregates and damaged organelles. Ribonuclease-recruiting chimeras achieve targeted RNA degradation, while the induced-proximity concept is repurposed for PTM regulation, enabling targeted glycosylation, acetylation, and phosphorylation and dephosphorylation via the recruitment of glycosyltransferases, acetyltransferases, and kinases and phosphatases. Future advances in all-small-molecule-based conditional systems, brain-targeted delivery, and regulatory frameworks informed by degradation kinetics will embed stimulus sensing and logic-gated operations into intelligent molecular systems, shifting the paradigm toward on-demand proteome and transcriptome rewiring for precision medicine.

title: Levetiracetam restores GABAergic function and network homeostasis following Vps35 deficiency in excitatory neurons.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRDs) remain incurable, partly due to their complex and poorly understood pathogenic mechanisms. Loss of vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein 35 (VPS35), a core component of the retromer complex, has been implicated in AD and ADRDs. While Vps35 deficiency is known to increase amyloidogenesis by regulating its cargo proteins, such as APP and BACE1, the precise mechanism by which VPS35 dysfunction leads to cognitive impairment remains elusive. While neuronal VPS35 regulates trafficking and functions of multiple synaptic membrane proteins, such as postsynaptic glutamatergic and GABAnergic receptors and pre-synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, and Levetiracetam (LEV), an antiepileptic drug that improves cognition, interacts with the SV2A, exactly how LEV enhances cognition is still a matter of debate. METHODS: Given the abundant expression of VPS35 in pyramidal excitatory neurons, we generated a conditional knockout mouse model with Vps35 deletion from postnatal glutamatergic excitatory neurons (Vps35CaMKIIα) and characterized its phenotypes using a combination of behavioral assessments, and electrophysiological, biochemical, and immunohiotological analyses in the hippocampal CA1 region. A targeted pharmacological screen was conducted to evaluate the therapeutic potential of LEV. RESULTS: Vps35 deletion did not disrupt the gross brain development but led to progressive cognitive decline beginning at three months of age. Electrophysiological analyses revealed earlier-onset hippocampal CA1 hyperexcitability, marked by depolarized resting membrane potentials and reduced Kir2.1 expression. However, restoring Kir2.1 to suppress hyperexcitability failed to rescue cognitive deficits. Instead, cognitive impairment was associated with weakened GABAergic transmission and disruption of the excitatory/inhibitory balance in the Schaffer collateral-CA1 circuit. Notably, LEV treatment diminished these deficits in mutant mice. Intriguingly, LEV increased the levels of retromer component, VPS26A, and multiple pre- and postsynaptic GABAergic proteins, in addition to SV2A, all of which were reduced in Vps35-deficient CA1 neurons. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify VPS35 in excitatory neurons as a critical factor for inhibitory synapse maintenance and network homeostasis. This study also highlights LEV as a potential therapeutic strategy for ADRDs through the preservation of GABAergic synapses.

title: Bridging the Translational Gap in Sex-Specific Alzheimer's Disease Using Human iPSC-Based Neural Cell Models.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits marked sex differences in disease prevalence, progression, and therapeutic responsiveness, with women disproportionately affected by both cognitive decline and neuropathological burden. Although sex hormones such as estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone have demonstrated neuroprotective effects in experimental systems, clinical outcomes of hormone-based interventions remain inconsistent. Emerging evidence further indicates that sex-specific molecular programs extend beyond endocrine signaling alone and include cell type-specific transcriptional architectures established across the lifespan. Recent single-cell transcriptomic studies have suggested that biological sex fundamentally shapes multicellular brain vulnerability. However, prevailing preclinical systems incompletely model human endocrine aging, sex chromosome biology, and patient-specific genetic heterogeneity, thereby limiting translational relevance. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neural systems provide a new platform for mechanistically interrogating sex-specific pathways within human genetic backgrounds. By preserving donor-specific genetic backgrounds and sex chromosome complement, iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes, microglia, and multicellular systems enable controlled investigation of hormone-responsive phenotypes, APOE-associated mechanisms, and cell type-specific transcriptional programs. However, their developmental immaturity and incomplete representation of systemic aging, vascular, immune, and endocrine physiology limit direct extrapolation to patients. Integration of these cellular systems with human omics datasets, neuropathological observations, and clinical studies may therefore help address specific components of the translational gap in AD.

title: Multi-omic profiling of 85 iPSC lines from familial dementia reveals cellular diversity and regulators of organoid development.
abstract: Systematic molecular characterization of human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines carrying disease-associated mutations is needed to distinguish disease-related biology from variation in cell state, genomic integrity, and genome-editing history, yet such systematic characterization is uncommon. Here, we profiled 85 human iPSC lines carrying MAPT mutations and isogenic controls using whole-genome sequencing, long-read sequencing of the MAPT locus, bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, and DNA methylation arrays. Single-cell analyses identified four reproducible iPSC states and candidate surface markers for their isolation. Whole-genome sequencing revealed unintended editing events and recurrent 20q11.21 duplications, which were associated with increased ID1 expression and impaired cortical organoid patterning. Transcriptomic analyses identified pathways associated with organoid quality and changes linked to clonal selection and editing, underscoring the need to use unconverted lines as isogenic controls. By providing an in-depth genomic characterization of MAPT iPSCs, this dataset serves as a proof of principle to enhance iPSC utility in biological research.

title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34-45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. Collectively, our findings suggest that the epitope accessibility and topology of EV-associated αSyn proteoforms, rather than their abundance alone, discriminate synucleinopathy subtypes, offering a framework for a blood-based conformational stratification of these disorders.

title: The Evolving Paradigm of Autism: Folate Receptor Autoimmunity deranging Epigenetic Programming in fetal and postnatal Brain Development.
abstract: This review on autism provides a summary of the multiple genetic, epigenetic and environmental changes setting the stage for disturbed brain development due to aberrant synaptogenesis and corticogenesis during the prenatal and post-natal periods. The emphasis is placed on nonmendelian transmission driven by epigenetics. Folate deficiency appears to play a critical role in influencing many of the structural changes contributing to developmental deficits. Impaired passage of folate across the placental and the blood-brain barriers to the fetal and postnatal brain because of folate receptor autoantibodies (FRAb) emerges as the major cause. Cerebral folate deficiency with or without autism has been associated with FOLR1 gene defects, a rare disorder. On the other hand, FRAb in association with low CSF folate is present in most children diagnosed with autism. These autoantibodies are present in more than 1/3 of asymptomatic parents of children with autism or are acquired by the child during the first two years of life. Early detection of FRAb amongst autistic children is necessary to enable high dose folinic acid treatment. The use of folinic acid before conception and during pregnancy among mothers or both parents with FRAb, represents a promising strategy to reduce the risk of autism in future offspring. Interventational treatments in parents prior to pregnancy and optimal therapeutic approaches in infants are needed to prevent disordered development of the pre- or post-natal brain.

title: The small giant actor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases: Microtubules.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a clinically and pathologically diverse group of disorders characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment, and neuronal loss. Although research has traditionally focused on disease-associated protein misfolding and aggregation, increasing evidence implicates abnormalities of cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport in several neurodegenerative conditions. Microtubules contribute to neuronal polarity, axonal and dendritic transport, organelle distribution, and synaptic maintenance. These functions are regulated in part by tubulin isotypes, post-translational modifications collectively described as the tubulin code, microtubule-associated proteins, and molecular motors. This narrative review examines evidence linking alterations in these processes with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease. We summarize proposed interactions among microtubule instability, impaired axonal transport, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disease-associated proteins, including tau, α-synuclein, mutant huntingtin, TDP-43, and prion protein. Evidence connecting tau pathology with microtubule dysfunction is comparatively well established in Alzheimer's disease and MAPT-related tauopathies, whereas findings in other disorders are more heterogeneous and are frequently derived from cellular or animal models. We also discuss emerging experimental approaches, candidate biomarkers, and investigational microtubule-directed treatments. However, no tubulin-specific biomarker or microtubule-targeted disease-modifying treatment discussed in this review has yet been clinically validated. Overall, microtubule dysfunction may represent one component of broader, disease-specific pathological networks rather than a universal primary cause of neurodegeneration. Further longitudinal and clinical studies are needed to determine whether microtubule-related alterations act as causes, consequences, or modifiers of disease progression.

title: Endosome-associated Rab GTPases control distinct aspects of neural circuit assembly.
abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

title: CHCHD2 mitigates age-associated proteostatic collapse by maintaining homeostasis of the mitochondria-lysosome axis.
abstract: Mutations in coiled-coil-helix-coiled-coil-helix domain containing 2 (CHCHD2), including the Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked CHCHD2T61I mutation, are associated with Lewy body disorders (LBDs) by unknown mechanisms. Here, we demonstrate that CHCHD2T61I exacerbates age-related brain pathologies, including axonal degeneration and cognitive deficits, by disrupting the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Specifically, CHCHD2T61I binds and reduces cathepsin B (CTSB) and cathepsin L (CTSL) levels, inducing lysosomal membrane permeability and impairing α-synuclein fibril clearance. We also demonstrate that human CHCHD2 declines in the brain with age, while expression of wild-type CHCHD2 safeguards against age-related neuroinflammation, dopaminergic neuron loss, insoluble protein aggregation, and structural deterioration of mitochondria and lysosomes. These findings, supported by observed reductions in CTSB and CHCHD2 in human LBD brains, establish CHCHD2 as a key regulator of neuronal resilience to aging and proteostatic collapse via the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Preventing age-associated CHCHD2 decline offers a therapeutic strategy to preserve brain health throughout aging.

title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

title: Neural Circuits of Social Behavior in Autism Spectrum Disorder: From Mechanism to Intervention.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Difficulties in social communication and interaction are core diagnostic features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet interventions targeting these difficulties have modest and variable effects. Understanding mechanistically distinct contributions to social behaviors may identify new therapeutic opportunities. METHODS: This narrative review integrates human neuroimaging studies, supporting rodent circuit neuroscience, clinical intervention research, and developmental studies. We organize the findings into four overlapping functional-computational domains and relate these domains to the Research Domain Criteria Social Processes framework. RESULTS: The four domains are: (1) Social Reward and Social Interest, encompassing the incentive and hedonic value of social contact and motivation to engage; (2) Social Memory and Social-Affective Value, encompassing recognition of familiar individuals and learned affective or motivational associations; (3) Social Cue Perception, Action Representation, and Social Prediction/Timing, encompassing the processing and forecasting of dynamic social information; and (4) Higher-Order Social Cognition and Model Updating, encompassing mental-state inference and the updating of person-specific social models. Because these domains are not independent, interactions among reward, memory, cue processing, prediction, and higher-order inference create multiple possible developmental entry points, such that early differences in one process may alter experience-dependent learning in others. Evidence for specific causal cascades remains preliminary and requires longitudinal testing. CONCLUSIONS: A circuit-and-development framework may improve hypothesis generation, domain-specific phenotyping, target-engagement assessment, and mechanism-aligned outcomes. Clinical translation, however, requires caution. Biomarkers should be validated as predictors of treatment response, cascade models should be tested longitudinally, and interventions should combine mechanism-informed targets with behavioral support that promotes generalization to daily life.

title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function. METHODS: We utilized healthy subjects and patients with SMA induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cultures to assess phenotypes occurring intrinsically within astrocyte processes (monocultures) and at the PAP-synaptic interface (co-cultures), respectively, using cell surface capture mass spectrometry proteomics, confocal and super resolution microscopy, synaptogliosome (SG) isolation, and electrophysiology. RESULTS: SMA astrocytes demonstrated intrinsic filopodia actin defects featuring low abundance of actin-associated cell surface N-glycoproteins, decreased filopodia density and CDC42-GTP levels after actin remodeling stimulation, and significantly reduced phosphorylated ezrin, radixin, and moesin (pERM) proteins. Within the SMA motor neuron and astrocyte co-cultures, we observed concurrent decreases in synapse number, actin-associated synapsin I expression, and PAP-associated expression of pERM proteins. Our dual treatment paradigm using SMN1 gene therapy combined with forskolin treatment to stimulate actin dynamics via increasing cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels resulted in increased branching and filopodia density of SMA astrocytes, and improved synapse formation and function of SMA motor neurons. INTERPRETATION: We define actin-associated defects impacting astrocyte filopodia dynamics and motor neuron synaptic function in SMA. This shaped our therapeutic approach targeted to SMN-dependent and actin-related disease mechanisms, which overall demonstrated improvements in motor neuron function and disease pathology. title: Human-Derived Motor Neuron Progenitor Cell Implantation Rescues Motor Endplates Following Peripheral Nerve Injury.
abstract: PURPOSE: Degradation of motor endplates (MEPs) following peripheral nerve injury (PNI) is a major determinant of functional recovery, as prolonged denervation renders target muscles progressively unreceptive to reinnervation. While prior studies have demonstrated that stem cell-based therapies may provide neurotrophic support following PNI, their potential effects on MEP preservation have not been well studied. We hypothesized that transplantation of human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived motor neuron progenitors (MNPs) into chronically denervated muscle would be associated with preservation of MEP architecture. METHODS: With Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee approval, chronic denervation injuries were created in mice via sciatic nerve transection. After 4 months of denervation, when MEPs have consistently degraded in this animal model, the denervated tibialis anterior (TA) was injected with low-dose MNPs (10,000 cells), high-dose MNPs (500,000 cells), or phosphate-buffered saline (negative control). Using a previously established method, hiPSCs were differentiated into functional MNPs prior to injection. At selected time points post-injection, the TA was harvested and immunostained to confirm MNP viability and detect the presence of MEPs. RESULTS: Transplanted MNPs remained viable within host muscle at both evaluated time points. No identifiable MEPs were detected in phosphate-buffered saline-treated chronically denervated muscle. In contrast, MNP-treated muscles demonstrated the presence of MEP-like structures following prolonged denervation. Qualitative differences in MEP density and morphologic complexity were observed between treatment groups, with greater preservation seen in the higher-dose cohort. Contralateral uninjured muscles demonstrated intact native MEP architecture. CONCLUSIONS: Intramuscular transplantation of hiPSC-derived MNPs into chronically denervated muscle was associated with preservation of MEP morphology in this preclinical proof-of-concept model. These preliminary findings suggest that cellular therapies may represent a potential adjunctive strategy to preserve end-organ receptivity following delayed peripheral nerve injury. TYPE OF STUDY/LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Preclinical controlled animal study, Level V.

title: TPPU, a soluble epoxide hydrolase inhibitor, mitigates Aβ-induced neurotoxicity via dual modulation of mitochondrial stabilization and JNK suppression.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, primarily driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) aggregation and neuronal apoptosis. This study aims to investigate the neuroprotective effects of soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) inhibition against Aβ-induced cytotoxicity in PC-12 cells, focusing on cell viability, apoptosis, and the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling pathway. Western blotting and fluorometric assays revealed elevated sEH expression and activity in Aβ1-42-treated PC-12 cells compared to untreated controls. Treatment with N-[1-(1-Oxopropyl)-4-piperidinyl]-N'-[4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenyl]urea (TPPU), a potent sEH inhibitor, significantly attenuated Aβ-induced apoptosis in PC-12 cells and enhanced cell viability. These findings were corroborated by CCK-8 assays and flow cytometry analyses. Furthermore, TPPU reversed Aβ-induced cleaved Caspase-3 dysregulation and restored mitochondrial membrane potential. Notably, exogenous administration of epoxyeicosatrienoic acids partially mimicked the protective effects of TPPU, primarily by preserving mitochondrial function. Western blot analysis confirmed that TPPU pretreatment suppressed the phosphorylation of JNK, thereby contributing to its anti-apoptotic effects. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that TPPU attenuates Aβ-induced neurotoxicity via dual mechanisms-restoring mitochondrial function and suppressing JNK activation-highlighting its potential as a therapeutic agent for AD.

title: KIF1A c.773C > T impairs neural progenitor differentiation and axonal transport in association with dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling.
abstract: Pathogenic KIF1A variants are established cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. However, the mechanisms by which they perturb early human neural development remains undefined. Here, we identified a heterozygous KIF1A c.773C > T (p.T258M) mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary spastic paraplegia and modeled its pathogenicity using patient-derived iPSCs and CRISPR-Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. We found that KIF1A-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) exhibited hyperproliferation, impaired cell-cycle exit, and defective neuronal differentiation, accompanied by defective neurite outgrowth, neuronal complexity, and calcium activity. Mechanistically, the KIF1A c.773C > T mutation compromised the binding affinity of KIF1A for β-tubulin and thereby impaired microtubule-associated localization of BDNF and synaptophysin. Integrated transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Notably, pharmacological activation of Wnt signaling restored BDNF expression, whereas exogenous BDNF rescued the proliferative and differentiative defects, indicating a potential functional relationship between BDNF and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Collectively, these findings suggested that dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling may serve as a contributory mechanism linking KIF1A motor dysfunction to aberrant neural stem cell fate.
